# SDET Quality Gate & Flake Repair Packet

## Constraint
- Non-negotiable: no daytime downtime on the checkout path (primary revenue).

## Risk Register (ranked by revenue impact)
| # | Risk                                  | Layer   | Kill-test (falsifiable)                         | Proof in CI                  |
|---|---------------------------------------|---------|-------------------------------------------------|------------------------------|
| 1 | Checkout submit silently fails        | browser | Playwright: assert order-confirmation locator   | trace.zip + screenshot       |
| 2 | Pricing/tax miscalculated             | unit    | assert total == subtotal+tax for boundary carts | jest report                  |
| 3 | Orders API contract drift             | api     | schema assert on POST /orders response          | contract-test JSON           |
| 4 | Checkout unusable by screen reader    | a11y    | axe scan: 0 serious violations on /checkout     | axe result artifact          |

## Selected approach
- Gate release on layers 1-4 in CI; quarantine flaky #1 until trace is deterministic.

## Rejected approach
- Re-run the whole browser suite until green ('retry until pass').
- Fails because: it hides flake instead of triaging it — a masked failure ships.

## Expected failure trigger
- Test #1 passes locally, fails in CI: hardcoded 500ms wait beats laptop, loses to CI.

## Reviewer objection
- 'Is risk-based test planning proven here, or merely described?'
- Answer: point to trace.zip for #1 and the axe artifact for #4 in the CI run.

steps.label: The constraint first
steps.note: Name the non-negotiable before any test. 'No daytime downtime on checkout' rules out a full-daytime reindex-style reset — the constraint must eliminate at least one option or it is decoration.

steps.label: Rank by revenue impact
steps.note: Checkout submit is #1 because a silent failure loses money directly. Ranking is the whole skill: you test the top risk at the cheapest layer that can catch its worst failure.

steps.label: One layer per risk
steps.note: Logic → unit, contract → API, user-flow → browser, conformance → a11y. Do not test a pricing bug through the browser; that is slow, flaky, and buries the signal.

steps.label: A falsifiable kill-test each
steps.note: Each row names a check that can return 'no'. 'Assert order-confirmation locator' fails loudly if checkout breaks — a test that can only pass is theater.

steps.label: Proof lives in CI
steps.note: trace.zip, axe artifact, contract JSON — evidence a reviewer replays, not 'it passed for me'. This is what separates covered from claimed-covered.

steps.label: Record the rejected approach
steps.note: 'Retry until green' is the seductive wrong answer: it converts a flaky signal into a false pass and ships a masked failure. Naming why it fails is required proof of judgment.

steps.label: The failure trigger
steps.note: A hardcoded 500ms wait that beats a fast laptop but loses to a loaded CI runner — the concrete cause of 'passes locally, fails in CI'.

risk-based-test-planning.caption: Run npx playwright test --trace=on so #1 produces trace.zip, and npx playwright show-report so a reviewer replays the CI failure instead of trusting a local pass.

risk-based-test-planning.question: A reviewer challenges: 'Is your risk-based test planning proven, or merely described?' Which packet answers the challenge?
options: One that lists best practices and reports the suite is 90% green locally.

One that re-runs the flaky checkout test until it passes and records the final green.

The others describe or hide — a local green bar (1), a retried-to-green flake (3), and abstract talk (4) all fail the 'proven not described' bar.

items: Every risk in the register maps to exactly one test layer, and you can defend why that layer is the cheapest one that catches its worst failure.
Each risk has a falsifiable kill-test — one that can return 'no' and fail the gate. If a check can only pass, it is theater; cut or replace it.
The proof for each risk is a CI artifact you can replay — Playwright trace.zip, axe result, or contract JSON — not 'it passed locally'.
The constraint actually constrains: name at least one coverage option it rules out (e.g. a full daytime browser reset on the revenue path).
The rejected approach ('retry until green') is recorded WITH the reason it fails: it masks a flaky failure instead of triaging it.
Run npx playwright test --trace=on and npx playwright show-report; confirm the trace opens and shows the exact step where checkout fails.

prompts: Explain why 'passes locally, fails in CI' is a planning failure, not just a code failure — using your own risk register as the example.
Walk a junior through why you tested the pricing risk at the unit layer instead of through the browser flow.
Point to the exact CI evidence that proves your top revenue risk is covered, and say what a reviewer would replay to verify it.

risk-based-test-planning.text: Risk-based planning is not a browser move — it is the move. In a regulated enterprise flow, the same register adds an audit-trail risk and the gate demands signed evidence; on a small team, you cut to the top two risks and one CI check, but the ranking discipline stays; at high scale, the browser layer thins and contract + observability tests carry more of the gate. What is invariant: rank by impact, bind each risk to the cheapest layer that can catch it, and prove coverage in CI. The sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md you built here is reused directly by the module capstone — it is the running artifact the rest of Quality Strategy And Risk Model grows.

Push a discount-math bug down to a unit test (milliseconds, deterministic), a "cart API rejects a stale price" bug to a contract test, and reserve the browser for the one thing only a browser proves: the user can actually complete the flow. Stacking everything at the top gives you a slow, flaky suite that fails in CI on timing and selectors — the exact failure this lesson exists to kill.

The pyramid is many fast unit tests; the trophy widens the integration/API band. Shape follows risk, never prestige.

# SDET Quality Gate & Flake Repair Packet

## Constraint
- Flow: guest checkout (revenue-critical, one-way door on a bad ship)
- Blocker: 6 flaky Playwright specs + untriaged a11y defects gate the release
- Non-negotiable: no manual sign-off; the CI gate decides ship/hold

## Portfolio (risk -> cheapest proving layer)
| Risk                          | Layer          | Kill-test                                  |
| discount math wrong           | unit           | assert total for known cart                |
| cart accepts stale price      | API / contract | contract test: POST stale price -> 409     |
| user cannot complete checkout | browser (E2E)  | 1 Playwright happy-path, role locator      |
| keyboard/contrast fails       | a11y           | axe scan on checkout, 0 serious/critical   |

## Chosen shape: trophy (wide contract band), NOT an E2E-heavy pyramid inverted
## Rejected: "cover checkout with 20 E2E specs" — slow, flaky, proves the same path 20x

## Flake repair rule (the fix)
- Ban CSS/text selectors -> use role locators + web-first assertions (auto-wait)
- await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' })).toBeEnabled()
- Evidence: npx playwright test --trace=on ; npx playwright show-report

## Reviewer objection answered
- "Is this proven or described?" -> trace.zip shows the retried step now deterministic

steps.label: Name the constraint first
steps.note: One-way door + "CI decides, no manual sign-off" sets the proof bar. A strategy that assumes a human will eyeball it is not a gate.

steps.label: Map each risk to its cheapest proving layer
steps.note: Discount math is deterministic logic — unit. Stale-price rejection is a contract — API. Only "user completes checkout" earns a browser test. This IS the pyramid/trophy decision, made concrete.

steps.label: Choose the shape and record the rejected one
steps.note: Trophy: the widest band is API/contract, because most checkout risk is integration, not pure logic or full-browser. The rejected E2E-heavy option is what caused the flake blocker.

steps.label: The flake-reduction rule — the actual repair
steps.note: Flakes come from brittle selectors + manual waits. Role locators + web-first assertions auto-wait, killing the "passes locally, fails in CI" timing race.

steps.label: Attach inspectable proof
steps.note: --trace=on + show-report turns "I fixed it" into a replayable trace.zip a reviewer can open. Described becomes proven.

test-pyramid-and-test-trophy.caption: A reviewer reads the table and can point to which layer proves each risk, then open the trace to confirm the flake is gone — not just claimed gone.

test-pyramid-and-test-trophy.text: The senior tell is where the WIDEST band sits, and why. Mike Cohn's pyramid puts it at unit; Kent C. Dodds' trophy widens the integration/API band because "tests that resemble the way users use the software give the most confidence per unit of flake." Neither is a law — the shape is an argument about where THIS product's risk actually lives. If your only justification is "pyramids are best practice," you copied a shape instead of choosing one.

test-pyramid-and-test-trophy.question: A reviewer challenges your checkout strategy: "Prove this is a portfolio, not just a coverage number." Which answer holds up?
options: "We hit 92% line coverage across the checkout service."

"Discount math is proven by unit tests, stale-price rejection by an API contract test, flow completion by one hardened Playwright spec with a role locator, and keyboard/contrast by an axe scan in CI — here is the trace and the axe report."
"We have 20 end-to-end tests covering every checkout screen."
"All tests are green, so the flow is safe to ship."
test-pyramid-and-test-trophy.explanation: Only option 2 maps each distinct risk to the cheapest layer that falsifies it and attaches inspectable evidence (trace + axe report). Coverage % (1) measures lines executed, not risks proven. Twenty E2E tests (3) is the flake-generating anti-pattern the lesson kills. "All green" (4) hides flaky-pass — a test that flips is green until the moment it matters.

test-pyramid-and-test-trophy.intro: Prove your portfolio holds — no vibes:
items: For every row in your risk table, name the layer AND the kill-test whose "no" would eliminate that risk. A row with no falsifiable check is a wish, not a test.
Confirm each risk sits on the CHEAPEST layer that can prove it — if logic-only risk is being checked in a browser, push it down and record why.
Run the browser tier with npx playwright test --trace=on and open the trace: the previously flaky step must now auto-wait via a web-first assertion, not a fixed sleep.
Confirm the accessibility check produces a concrete pass/fail (axe: 0 serious/critical on the checkout flow), not "looks accessible".
Check the CI gate decision is mechanical: given the four layer results, ship/hold is determined by rule, not by a human glancing at a dashboard.

prompts: In your own words: why does assigning a risk to the wrong layer (e.g. logic risk to a browser test) produce the exact "passes locally, fails in CI" flake this lesson is about?
Explain when you'd choose a trophy (wide API/contract band) over a classic pyramid, using your checkout portfolio as the example.
Point to the single flake-reduction rule in your packet and explain why a role locator plus a web-first assertion is more deterministic than a CSS selector plus a fixed wait.

test-pyramid-and-test-trophy.text: The move is portfolio-thinking, not Playwright: assign each risk to the cheapest instrument that can falsify it, and reserve the slow, expensive instrument for what only it can prove. A hospital doesn't MRI every patient — it triages by which test rules out the most danger per dollar; a security team layers cheap static scans under expensive pen-tests. Carry your sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md into the module capstone: it is the artifact your risk register, defect report, and CI gate result all hang from. In a stricter environment — a regulated payments flow — the shape holds but the a11y and contract bands widen and the gate demands signed evidence. You don't just argue pyramid-vs-trophy now; you can map a real release's risk to layers and prove the gate.

release-confidence-model.prompt: A browser test failed in CI but passes when you re-run it. The fastest path to a green pipeline is to click 'Retry' until it passes. What does that actually decide? Answer before reading on.

A flaky test that passes on retry has not been triaged — you have not separated a real regression from a timing/selector/fixture problem, you have only rolled the dice until you liked the number. Retry-to-green trains the pipeline to hide exactly the signal a release gate exists to catch. The expert move is flake triage: read the trace, classify the failure (real defect vs. environment assumption), then decide — not re-run until the anxiety stops.

## Constraint
- Ship blocked: 2 flaky Playwright tests + 4 untriaged a11y defects on /checkout
- Non-negotiable: no ship without replayable evidence per failing check

## Flake autopsy (npx playwright test --trace=on)
- checkout.spec: 'Place order' click races the button's enabled state
- Root cause: getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }).click() fires pre-hydration
- Repair: await expect(locator).toBeEnabled() BEFORE click — assert state, not timing

## Selected approach
- Gate = unit(pass) + contract(pass) + browser(triaged, retry=0) + a11y(triaged)
- Retries pinned to 0 in CI so a pass is a pass, not a re-roll

## Rejected approach
- retries: 2 in CI to force green — hides the race, ships on noise

## Verification
- trace.zip + video.webm attached; axe scan: 4 defects -> 2 fixed, 2 waived w/ owner+date

## Gate decision: HOLD until toBeEnabled() repair lands; then SHIP
## Invalidation: any real defect surviving triage flips SHIP -> HOLD

steps.label: Constraint before solution
steps.note: Name the operating constraint first: what blocks the ship and what is non-negotiable. Evidence per failing check is the bar the whole gate defends.

steps.label: The flake autopsy
steps.note: npx playwright test --trace=on turns 'it's flaky' into a named cause: the click races hydration. This is triage — separating a real timing bug from random noise.

steps.label: Assert state, not timing
steps.note: toBeEnabled() before click is the flake-reduction rule: web-first assertions wait on the condition, killing the race. Never sprinkle waitForTimeout.

steps.label: Selected approach + retries=0
steps.note: Pinning CI retries to 0 is the move that makes the gate honest — a pass means the flow is stable, not that it eventually passed.

steps.label: The rejected option, recorded
steps.note: Writing down retries:2 and WHY it fails (ships on noise) is what makes the decision inspectable instead of merely described.

steps.label: Verification + invalidation
steps.note: Trace, video, and axe results are the replayable proof; the invalidation line states exactly what flips SHIP back to HOLD. That line is the packet's spine.

release-confidence-model.caption: A reviewer opens trace.zip, replays the pre-hydration click, confirms toBeEnabled() removes the race, and reads the gate decision — no narration needed.

release-confidence-model.text: The senior tell in a release meeting: they gate on the flake they EXPECT to be noise, and still open the trace. Retries hide races; a web-first assertion (toBeEnabled, toBeVisible) waits on the actual condition and turns a flaky test into a deterministic one. If your green pipeline needs retries to stay green, you do not have confidence — you have a coin flip with a nice color.

A screenshot of the pipeline showing a green checkmark.
A list of every test in the suite and its last run status.

A green checkmark (3) can be a retry artifact; a strategy paragraph (1) is description, not proof; a test inventory (4) shows coverage, not that the flaky failure was triaged rather than re-rolled.

release-confidence-model.intro: Prove your release confidence model holds — no green-vibe:
items: Every failing check in the packet has a triage verdict: real defect (hold) or environment assumption (repair). If any failure was cleared by re-running, re-triage it with npx playwright test --trace=on.
The flake repair asserts a state (toBeEnabled/toBeVisible), not a timing (waitForTimeout). Confirm CI retries are pinned to 0 so a pass is a pass.
The rejected approach is written down with the reason it fails under operational evidence — not just the option you chose.
At least one inspection-hook output is attached: trace.zip, npx playwright show-report, or a video/screenshot the reviewer can open.
The invalidation condition is explicit: name the exact result that flips your SHIP decision back to HOLD.

prompts: In your own words: why does re-running a flaky test until it passes destroy the signal a release gate exists to capture?
Explain the difference between asserting a state and waiting on a timing, using your own flake repair as the example.
Point to the exact evidence in your packet that proves the checkout flow is safe to ship — and name what would make that evidence invalid.

release-confidence-model.text: The same model scales by changing the stakes, not the shape. On a small team, the gate might be one Playwright smoke + a manual a11y pass, and 'evidence' is a shared trace link. In a regulated enterprise, the gate hardens: signed test evidence, contract tests as a merge blocker, WCAG conformance recorded per release, and an audit trail the invalidation condition maps to a change-control ticket. At high scale, flake triage becomes an automated quarantine lane and the gate reads a stability score across thousands of runs. What stays invariant everywhere: risk mapped to the cheapest disqualifying proof, and no ship without replayable evidence. This packet is your capstone seed — the capstone reuses this exact sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md and its proof; if it can't be reused there, it isn't premium-ready yet.

defect-taxonomy.outcome: Take the release blocked by flaky browser tests and untriaged accessibility defects, and build a defect taxonomy: sort every failure into a named class (product bug, flaky test, environment drift, accessibility conformance gap), then write the release decision it forces. Ship the decision packet.
defect-taxonomy.proof: sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md with a defect classification table (each failure → class → evidence → owner → gate action), the rejected option, an expected CI failure, and a reviewer objection response. A reviewer can point to one row and replay why it was classed as flake, not bug.
defect-taxonomy.unlock: Every failure in your packet is assigned a defect class with evidence attached, and the class dictates a gate action (block, quarantine, or file) — no failure sits untriaged.
defect-taxonomy.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have a taxonomy if 'flaky' is a shrug for every red test. A test called flaky without a trace, a retry-variance number, or a root cause is a real bug you are shipping past. The class is a claim you must be able to defend, not a place to hide a failure.

defect-taxonomy.text: Release train leaves in an hour, the pipeline is a wall of red, and the room splits: half say 'the tests are just flaky, override the gate,' half say 'those reds are real, hold the release.' Nobody has sorted which is which — so the loudest voice, not the evidence, is about to decide whether a broken checkout ships.

A red CI run is not one thing — it is product bugs, flaky tests, environment drift, and accessibility gaps tangled together, each demanding a different response. Defect taxonomy is the sort that turns an undifferentiated wall of red into a release decision another reviewer can inspect.

defect-taxonomy.prompt: A browser test fails in CI but passes when you re-run it locally. Is that a flaky test? Decide before reading on.
defect-taxonomy.reveal: Not proven yet — 'passes on my machine' is the single most expensive misdiagnosis in QA. It could be a flaky test (timing/locator race), but it could equally be environment drift (CI has different data, viewport, or a slow network the local run doesn't) or a real bug that only the CI data exposes. Calling it flake because it's inconvenient re-runs it green and ships the defect. The class is decided by evidence — a trace, a retry-variance rate, a diff of environments — never by where it happened to pass.

defect-taxonomy.title: A taxonomy sorts every failure into a class that dictates a gate action
defect-taxonomy.text: Assign each failure one class — product bug, flaky test, environment drift, or accessibility conformance gap — backed by evidence. The class chooses the action: bug blocks, flake quarantines, drift fixes the harness, a11y gap files against conformance. Untriaged is not a class.

defect-taxonomy.title: The defect triage tree — one red run, four classes, four gate actions
defect-taxonomy.subtitle: Every CI failure enters at the top and must exit through exactly one class. The evidence question at each fork decides the branch; the accessibility gap and the flake are the two the room most wants to skip. This is the failure path (untriaged override) and the repair path (evidence-sorted gate) in one tree.

defect-taxonomy.title: Building the classification table, one row at a time
defect-taxonomy.subtitle: The heart of sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md — every failure sorted, evidenced, and turned into a gate action.
defect-taxonomy.code:
# SDET Quality Gate & Flake Repair Packet
## Defect Classification Table
| id | failing check              | class          | evidence (inspection hook)                       | owner   | gate action        |
|----|----------------------------|----------------|--------------------------------------------------|---------|--------------------|
| D1 | checkout.spec: total wrong | product bug    | trace.zip: assert 40.00 != 44.00 (tax) every run | payments| BLOCK release      |
| D2 | login.spec: timeout        | flaky test     | 3/10 fail; trace shows locator race, no code diff | qa      | quarantine + FLK-88|
| D3 | search.spec: 0 results     | env drift      | CI seed DB empty; passes with fixture seeded      | infra   | fix harness, re-run|
| D4 | cart: button 2.1:1 contrast| a11y gap       | axe-core: color-contrast on primary CTA          | design  | file A11Y-12, block|
## Rejected option
- Retry-all-3x-then-pass: hides D1 and D4 behind green; ships a real bug + WCAG fail
## Expected CI failure if taxonomy is skipped
- tests pass locally but fail in CI: D3 selectors/seed assumptions weak → false 'flaky' label
## Reviewer objection + response
- Q: is D2 proven flaky or just re-run green? A: retry-variance 3/10 + trace race, ticket FLK-88

steps.label: D1 — the real bug the room called flake
steps.note: It fails deterministically every run with the same assertion (tax miscalculated). Deterministic + reproducible = product bug. This one BLOCKS. Misclass it as flake and you ship broken checkout.

steps.label: D2 — an honest flake, with proof
steps.note: 3/10 failures, no code change, trace shows a locator race — that is the evidence that earns the 'flaky' label. Quarantine it AND file FLK-88; a flake without a ticket is a bug in waiting.

steps.label: D3 — environment drift, not the test's fault
steps.note: The CI seed DB is empty; seed the fixture and it passes. This is the 'passes locally, fails in CI' trap from the pretest — the harness is wrong, not the code. Fix the harness, don't retry.

steps.label: D4 — the accessibility gap nobody triaged
steps.note: axe-core flags 2.1:1 contrast on the primary CTA — below WCAG 1.4.3's 4.5:1. It is a conformance defect with its own class and its own gate action: file A11Y-12 and block.

steps.label: The rejected option, on the record
steps.note: 'Retry 3x then pass' is the seductive shortcut. Writing why it fails (hides D1 and D4) is what makes the packet inspectable instead of a defense of a guess.

steps.label: The reviewer objection, answered in the artifact
steps.note: The whole taxonomy stands or falls on whether 'flaky' is defensible. Attach the retry-variance number and the trace so a reviewer can replay the classification, not take it on faith.

defect-taxonomy.caption: A reviewer reads any row and can replay the classification from the evidence column — that is the difference between a triaged gate and a blind override.

defect-taxonomy.title: Two responses to the same red pipeline
defect-taxonomy.subtitle: Release blocked, N reds, one hour left. Both feel like a decision; only one is inspectable.

Retry 3x; whatever goes green is 'passing'
No class, no trace, no retry-variance number
Accessibility failures ignored as noise
Ships D1 (tax bug) and D4 (WCAG fail) to prod
left.verdict: A guess wearing a gate's clothes

Evidence attached: trace.zip, retry rate, axe output
Class dictates action: block / quarantine / fix / file

right.verdict: A decision a reviewer can replay

defect-taxonomy.caption: The flake bucket is where real bugs go to ship. A defect class is a claim backed by evidence, never a place to park an inconvenient red.

defect-taxonomy.text: The senior tell: a strong SDET separates signal from noise by writing down what was directly observed (the trace, the axe violation), what was inferred (a locator race), and what would invalidate the call (D2 fails 8/10 next week → it was never flaky, it was a bug). WCAG 1.4.3 makes contrast a hard conformance line, not an opinion — 4.5:1 for normal text — so an accessibility gap is a defect class with a spec behind it, not a design preference.

defect-taxonomy.question: A reviewer challenges: 'You labeled D2 a flaky test and quarantined it. Prove it's flake and not a bug you're hiding.' Which response actually proves the classification?
options: "It passed when I re-ran the pipeline, so it must be flaky."
"It fails 3 of 10 runs with no code change, the trace shows a locator resolving before the element renders, and it's tracked as FLK-88 for a fix."
"Everyone on the team agrees login tests are always flaky."
"I set retries to 3 so it's green now — we can move on."
defect-taxonomy.explanation: Only option 2 attaches evidence that separates flake from bug: a retry-variance rate (3/10), a trace showing the race condition as the mechanism, and a tracking ticket so the flake is repaired, not just buried. 'Re-ran green' (1) and 'set retries to 3' (4) are exactly how a real bug gets shipped past the gate; 'everyone agrees' (3) is folklore, not proof. A defect class must be replayable from evidence.

defect-taxonomy.intro: Prove your taxonomy holds — no vibes:
items: Every failing check has exactly one class assigned. If any red is still 'untriaged' or 'misc', it is not sorted — the gate cannot be trusted.
Every 'flaky test' row carries a retry-variance number (e.g. 3/10) AND a trace or a ticket. A flake asserted without evidence is a bug you are about to ship.
At least one accessibility failure is classified with its axe rule / WCAG criterion (e.g. color-contrast, 1.4.3), not folded into 'test noise'.
Each class maps to a distinct gate action (block / quarantine / fix harness / file). If two classes trigger the same reflex, you have not really distinguished them.
You captured output from at least two inspection hooks (npx playwright test --trace=on, npx playwright show-report) so a reviewer can replay a classification without your narration.
You wrote the invalidation condition: the observation that would prove a class wrong (D2 fails 8/10 next week → it was a bug, not a flake).

prompts: In your own words: why is 'passes on retry' evidence of nothing on its own, and what three things would you need to defensibly call a test flaky?
Walk a junior through your classification table: pick the row that most tempted you to mislabel, and explain the evidence that fixed the class.
Explain why an accessibility conformance gap needs its own defect class and gate action instead of being triaged as a normal browser-test failure.

defect-taxonomy.text: The same sort travels anywhere failures pile up faster than you can respond to them. A support org triages tickets into bug / user-error / feature-request / outage — each with a different owner and SLA — before touching one, because an unsorted queue is decided by whoever shouts. A hospital ED runs triage classes before treatment for the identical reason. Change the environment and the classes shift but the discipline is invariant: sort by evidence, let the class dictate the action, never let 'it's probably nothing' be a class. Carry this packet into the capstone — the release gate you build there reuses this exact classification table and its flake/a11y evidence, because a gate that cannot tell a bug from a flake is not a gate, it is a coin flip.

unit-integration-boundary.outcome: Take one revenue-critical web flow (checkout, signup, or a real one you own) and assign each behavior to the RIGHT test layer — unit for logic, contract for API shape, browser for the user-visible flow — then write the boundary rule that says why a check lives where it does. Produce the decision section of sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md.
unit-integration-boundary.proof: Section 1 ("Layer Assignment") of sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md: a table mapping 4+ behaviors to unit / contract / browser, each with a one-line reason, plus one behavior you DEMOTED from browser to a lower layer and why. A reviewer agrees no behavior is tested at a heavier layer than it needs.
unit-integration-boundary.unlock: Your packet assigns every behavior to the lightest layer that can prove it, names the boundary rule, and demotes at least one over-heavy browser test.
unit-integration-boundary.doNotClaim: Do not claim you "have good coverage" because a Playwright test touches the behavior. A browser test that re-verifies pure logic is a slow, flaky duplicate of a unit test — coverage at the wrong layer is a liability, not an asset.

unit-integration-boundary.text: A revenue-critical checkout release is blocked: 40 Playwright tests are red, the on-call has re-run the suite four times to "see if it passes," and nobody can say whether the app is broken or the tests are. Every one of those 40 asserts pure pricing logic through a real browser — the boundary was never drawn.

This opens Automation Foundations because every later skill — flake triage, contract tests, CI quality gates — assumes each behavior already lives at the right layer. Draw the unit/integration boundary wrong and you inherit a slow, flaky suite that fails in CI for reasons that have nothing to do with the product.

unit-integration-boundary.prompt: A checkout applies a 10%-off coupon. Where do you test that the discounted total is correct — in a Playwright browser test that clicks through the whole flow, or somewhere else? Answer before reading on.
unit-integration-boundary.reveal: Somewhere else. "Discounted total = subtotal × 0.9" is pure logic — it needs a unit test that runs in milliseconds, not a 12-second browser test that boots a server, renders a page, and can flake on a slow selector. The browser test's job is narrower: prove the user can reach checkout and SEE a total, not re-derive the arithmetic. Testing logic through the browser is the #1 source of "passes locally, flakes in CI."

unit-integration-boundary.title: Test each behavior at the lightest layer that can prove it
unit-integration-boundary.text: Unit tests own logic (fast, isolated). Contract tests own API shape between services. Browser tests own the user-visible flow only. The boundary rule: push every check DOWN to the lightest layer that still proves it. Heavier-than-needed = slow and flaky.

unit-integration-boundary.title: The test pyramid on a real checkout flow
unit-integration-boundary.subtitle: Each behavior sits at exactly one layer. Logic pushed down runs in milliseconds and never flakes; only the thin user-visible flow reaches the browser. The stale-selector edge is where CI flake is born.

unit-integration-boundary.title: The same behavior tested at three layers — each doing only its job
unit-integration-boundary.subtitle: Discount logic (unit), API shape (contract), user flow (browser). Notice what each one does NOT re-assert.

steps.label: Unit owns the math
steps.note: applyDiscount is a pure function — assert it directly, including the empty-cart edge. This runs in milliseconds and can never flake on a selector.

steps.label: Contract owns the shape
steps.note: The contract test proves /api/checkout returns { total: number } — the agreement between frontend and backend. It checks SHAPE, deliberately not the value; the value is already proven at the unit layer.

steps.label: Browser owns the flow
steps.note: The browser test proves a shopper can navigate to checkout and SEE a total render. getByRole and getByTestId are resilient locators — no brittle CSS chains.

steps.label: What it does NOT assert
steps.note: It never re-checks that the total equals 90. That would drag pure logic into a 12-second flake-prone browser run — the exact boundary violation this lesson kills.

unit-integration-boundary.caption: Three tests, one behavior, zero overlap. The value is proven once (unit), the boundary once (contract), the flow once (browser). Delete any layer and you lose signal; duplicate one and you buy flake.

unit-integration-boundary.title: Same coverage goal, two suites
unit-integration-boundary.subtitle: Both "test checkout." One is a 4-second unit-heavy suite; one is a 6-minute browser wall that flakes in CI.

left.label: Everything through the browser
lines: 40 Playwright tests re-assert pricing math
Each boots a server + renders a page (~12s)
Discount edge cases clicked through the UI
Brittle CSS locators: div.total > span:nth-child(2)
Passes locally, flakes in CI on timing + selectors
left.verdict: Slow, flaky, blocks releases for non-bugs

right.label: Boundary-drawn suite
lines: Pricing math → 30 unit tests (milliseconds, no I/O)
API shape → 3 contract tests at /api/checkout
User flow → 4 browser tests, getByRole/getByTestId
Edge cases live at the unit layer where they belong
Same behaviors covered; suite runs in seconds, stable
right.verdict: Fast, stable, red only when the product is truly broken

unit-integration-boundary.caption: Coverage is not the score — coverage AT THE RIGHT LAYER is. A browser test that re-proves unit logic adds latency and flake with no new signal. Push it down.

unit-integration-boundary.text: The senior tell: before writing any test, a strong SDET asks "what is the CHEAPEST layer that can falsify this?" A flaky suite is almost never a Playwright problem — it is a boundary problem, logic that leaked up into the browser. Fix the boundary and most of your flake disappears before you ever touch waits or retries. This is the flake-reduction rule the whole course leans on.

unit-integration-boundary.question: A reviewer challenges: "Prove your discount rule is correct." Which test is the RIGHT evidence — and why?
options: A Playwright test that adds items, applies the coupon, and screenshots the total — because it exercises the real UI.
A unit test asserting applyDiscount(100, 0.1) === 90 plus the empty-cart edge — because the rule is pure logic, so it belongs at the fastest, non-flaky layer.
A contract test on /api/checkout that checks the response has a total field — because that is where checkout happens.
No test is needed if the number looks right in staging.
unit-integration-boundary.explanation: The discount rule is pure logic, so its proof belongs at the unit layer: fast, isolated, and it can never flake on a selector or a slow render. The browser test (1) is slow and re-proves nothing new; the contract test (3) verifies SHAPE not VALUE; "looks right" (4) is not evidence. Right-layer proof is the point of the boundary.

unit-integration-boundary.intro: Prove your layer assignment holds — no vibes:
items: For every browser test in your packet, name one thing it asserts that CANNOT be proven at a lower layer. If you can't, demote it — it is a duplicate.
Run npx playwright test --project=chromium and confirm each browser test asserts a user-visible flow (a page loads, an element renders), not a computed value.
Confirm your logic edge cases (empty cart, zero total, invalid coupon) live at the unit layer, where they run in milliseconds.
Confirm at least one contract test pins the /api/checkout request+response shape, so the browser layer can trust the API instead of re-verifying it.
Capture npx playwright test --trace=on for one browser test and confirm the trace shows a flow, not arithmetic — the trace is your CI-gate evidence.

prompts: In your own words: why does testing pure logic through a browser create the "passes locally, flakes in CI" failure this course keeps warning about?
Explain the difference between a contract test checking SHAPE and a unit test checking VALUE, using your own checkout as the example.
Name one behavior you DEMOTED from the browser layer, where it landed, and what you gained by moving it.

unit-integration-boundary.text: The boundary is domain-independent: at a smaller team you may fold contract tests into unit tests and keep a razor-thin browser layer; in a regulated enterprise you add an accessibility-conformance layer and a mandatory CI quality gate on top; at high scale you shard the browser layer and let contract tests guard every service seam. What stays invariant everywhere: push each check to the lightest layer that can prove it. Next lesson keeps this exact sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md and adds the flake-triage section — because now that logic lives at the right layer, the browser tests that DO remain must be made deterministic.

api-contract-tests.outcome: Take one revenue-critical API your web flow depends on and write an API contract test: pin the request shape, the response schema, and status codes so that when the provider drifts, the CONTRACT fails loud and cheap — before a flaky browser test discovers it slow and expensive in CI.
api-contract-tests.proof: sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md with a runnable contract test: named endpoint, a schema assertion (not just status 200), the drift you're guarding against, the CI-gate decision it feeds, plus the rejected option and one reviewer objection. A reviewer can replay the failure: break the schema, watch the contract test go red in seconds.
api-contract-tests.unlock: Your contract test asserts response SHAPE (fields, types, required, status), fails on provider drift, and names what it deliberately does NOT test.
api-contract-tests.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have a contract test if your assertion is only `expect(res.status).toBe(200)`. A 200 with a renamed field or a null where a number was promised still passes — and your UI still breaks. Status-only is a smoke check wearing a contract's clothes.

api-contract-tests.text: Green pipeline, confident deploy — then checkout dies in production because the payments API quietly renamed `amount_cents` to `amountMinor`. Your browser tests didn't catch it: they timed out on a spinner that never resolved, and the team spent the night blaming Playwright instead of the contract nobody pinned.

A browser test that fails because an API changed shape is expensive, slow, and points at the wrong layer — you debug the UI when the provider drifted. The API contract test is the cheap, fast tripwire one level down: it catches drift at the seam, so the release decision rests on the right evidence.

api-contract-tests.prompt: Your API test asserts `res.status === 200` and passes. The provider renamed a field from `total` to `grand_total`. Does your test go red? Answer before reading on.
api-contract-tests.reveal: No — and that's the trap. The response is still a well-formed 200; only its SHAPE changed. Status-only assertions test that the server answered, not that it answered with the contract you built against. The UI reads `data.total`, gets `undefined`, and renders `$NaN` — while your test stays green. A contract test asserts the schema (fields present, types correct, required non-null), so a rename fails LOUD at the API layer instead of silently at the customer's screen.

api-contract-tests.title: A contract test pins the SHAPE of the exchange, not just that it happened
api-contract-tests.text: Assert request and response against a schema: fields present, types correct, required non-null, status codes explicit. When the provider drifts, the contract fails fast at the seam — one level below the browser test, cheaper to run and unambiguous to read.

api-contract-tests.title: Where the contract test sits: the tripwire below the browser test
api-contract-tests.subtitle: A provider rename hits three checks. The contract test fails FAST and points at the seam; the browser test fails SLOW and points at the wrong layer; production fails on the customer. Guard the cheapest one.

nodes.label: Contract test
nodes.description: schema assert · fields · types · required · status

nodes.label: Browser test

legend.label: contract test — the cheap tripwire at the seam

api-contract-tests.title: Writing the contract test, one assertion at a time
api-contract-tests.subtitle: A real Playwright API contract test with a Zod schema — the artifact from sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md.

steps.label: Declare the contract as a schema
steps.note: This is the exact shape the UI reads. `amount_cents` is `number().int()` — a rename or a string here MUST fail. The schema IS the contract, versioned in the test.

steps.label: Pin the field the UI actually depends on
steps.note: The checkout renders `amount_cents`. If the provider renames it, `safeParse` fails — the failure the pretest exposed, caught at the seam instead of on the customer's screen.

steps.label: Status is a first-class assertion
steps.note: 201 Created, not 200. A provider that silently downgrades to 200 changed the contract; assert the exact code, not `< 400`.

steps.label: Assert shape, never just status
steps.note: `safeParse` is the whole point: it checks every field, type, and required constraint at once. `expect(status).toBe(200)` alone would have passed the drift the pretest described.

steps.label: Fail with the reason attached
steps.note: Passing `parsed.error` into the assertion message means a red test SAYS which field drifted — a reviewer replays it in seconds, no debugging the UI.

api-contract-tests.caption: Break it to prove it: rename `amount_cents` → `amountMinor` in the API and this test goes red at line 20 naming the exact field — fast, cheap, unambiguous.

api-contract-tests.title: Weak vs gold: the same API test
api-contract-tests.subtitle: Both hit the endpoint. Only one is a contract that catches drift.

left.label: Smoke check disguised as a contract
lines: `expect(res.status()).toBe(200)` and nothing else
A renamed field still returns 200 → stays GREEN
No schema: types, required, enums unchecked
Drift leaks past CI into the browser test — or prod
When it fails, it says nothing about WHY
left.verdict: Green while the UI renders $NaN — false confidence

right.label: Real API contract test
lines: Asserts full response schema (fields · types · required)
Status code pinned exactly (201, not `< 400`)
A rename or type change fails FAST at the seam
Failure message names the exact field that drifted
Documents what it does NOT test (out-of-scope boundary)
right.verdict: Red in seconds, points at the provider — trustworthy gate

api-contract-tests.caption: The gold version is inspectable: a reviewer can break the schema, watch it fail, and read which field moved. The weak version can only say 'the server answered.'

api-contract-tests.text: The senior move is knowing which test layer OWNS a failure. When a field renames, the contract test should go red — not the browser test. If your only signal is a flaky Playwright timeout on a spinner, you'll debug selectors and waits for an hour before realizing the API drifted. Push the assertion down to the cheapest layer that can prove it: that's how you turn flake triage into a five-second read.

api-contract-tests.question: A reviewer challenges: 'How do I know this is a contract test and not a smoke test?' Which evidence answers them?
options: The test hits the real endpoint and asserts `res.status() === 200`.
The test parses the response against a schema (fields, types, required, exact status), and a field rename in the provider makes it fail with the drifted field named.
The test runs in CI and is green right now.
The test retries three times to reduce flakiness before passing.
api-contract-tests.explanation: A contract test proves the exchange's SHAPE. Only option 2 shows an assertion that fails on drift and names what drifted — the falsifiable proof. Status-only (1) passes through renames; being green now (3) proves nothing about drift; retrying (4) masks signal rather than pinning the contract, and can hide real breakage.

api-contract-tests.intro: Prove your contract test is real — no vibes:
items: Break the provider on purpose: rename one field the UI reads. Your test must go RED and name that field. If it stays green, you asserted status, not shape.
Confirm at least one assertion checks TYPE and REQUIRED, not just presence — a `null` where a number was promised should fail.
Confirm the status code is pinned exactly (e.g. 201), not a loose `< 400` or missing entirely.
Run it in CI and confirm a red contract test BLOCKS the gate — a decision, not a warning that scrolls past.
Write the out-of-scope line: name one thing this test deliberately does NOT cover (auth, rate limits, pagination) so the boundary is defended, not accidental.

prompts: Explain to a teammate why `expect(res.status()).toBe(200)` is a smoke check, not a contract — using the field-rename failure as your example.
Why should a provider rename fail the CONTRACT test and not the BROWSER test? What does pushing the assertion down one layer buy you in flake triage?
Point to the exact line in your artifact that would go red on drift, and say which field it names.

api-contract-tests.text: The move — pin the shape of a seam so drift fails fast and cheap — travels the whole stack. Consumer-driven contracts (Pact) let a frontend team publish the shape they depend on so the provider's CI breaks the moment it drifts. JSON Schema guards event payloads on a queue; OpenAPI validation guards a public API's responses. Same discipline every time: assert the contract at the cheapest layer that can prove it, name the blast radius, defend the boundary. Carry this artifact — sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md — into the capstone: it's the evidence that your green pipeline means the release is safe, not just that the servers answered.

fixture-design.outcome: Take a revenue-critical web flow whose release is blocked by flaky Playwright tests, and design the fixtures that kill the flake: a scoped, deterministic setup layer with an explicit teardown and a single source of test state. Write it down as a decision packet a reviewer can replay.
fixture-design.proof: sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md: the constraint (what makes the flow flaky), the chosen fixture scope + strategy, the rejected option, the failure trigger you reproduced, the verification hook output (a --trace=on run), and a transfer note. A reviewer can point to the constraint, replay the failure, and evaluate the repair.
fixture-design.unlock: Your packet names the flake's operational cause, the fixture scope that removes it, a falsifiable verification hook, and the rejected alternative — with no step that only works on your machine.
fixture-design.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'designed fixtures' if the artifact only describes good practices. Passing locally is not proof. A fixture design is only proven when you show the CI failure it prevents and the trace that confirms the repair. Description without a replayed failure is theater.

fixture-design.text: Green locally, red in CI, for the third release in a row — the checkout suite fails on a login step that works every time on your laptop. The room is one click from disabling the test and shipping blind, because nobody owns the state the test starts from.

A fixture is the deterministic world a test wakes up in — the seeded user, the authenticated session, the clean database, the mocked clock. Fixture design is where flake is won or lost: get the scope and teardown right and the same test passes locally and in CI; get it wrong and you ship on false confidence.

fixture-design.prompt: Your login test passes locally but fails ~1 in 5 runs in CI. Your instinct is to add a `waitForTimeout(2000)` before the assertion. Before you do — what does that actually fix? Answer first.
fixture-design.reveal: Nothing — it hides the symptom and adds two seconds to every run. A hard sleep treats a state problem as a timing problem. The real cause is almost always the fixture: the test shares an authenticated session, a leftover cart, or a user another test mutated. The flake is not in the assertion; it is in the world the test started from. Fix the fixture scope and the sleep becomes unnecessary.

fixture-design.title: A fixture is deterministic, scoped state with a guaranteed teardown
fixture-design.text: Design each fixture to answer three things: what state it provides, how wide it is shared (per-test vs per-worker), and how it is torn down. The invariant: no test may depend on state another test left behind. Isolation is the whole job.

fixture-design.title: The fixture lifecycle — where flake enters and where isolation kills it
fixture-design.subtitle: A test's world is built by fixtures, exercised, then torn down. The suspect edge is shared, un-scoped state leaking across tests. Per-test isolation cuts that edge; the CI trace is the evidence.

legend.label: the suspect edge — shared state leaking

fixture-design.title: The fixture that ends the login flake
fixture-design.subtitle: A Playwright fixture: worker-scoped seed for cost, per-test auth for isolation, teardown after `use`. This is the artifact from the decision packet.

steps.label: Unique state per test
steps.note: A timestamp+random email means every test gets its own user. This alone removes the leading flake class: two tests fighting over one shared account's cart.

steps.label: Seed via API, not the UI
steps.note: seedUser hits the backend directly. Building state through the browser is slow and is itself a flake source — you are testing setup, not the flow.

steps.label: The `use` handoff
steps.note: Everything before `use` is setup; the test runs during `use`. This is Playwright's fixture contract — the seam between world-building and the test body.

steps.label: Teardown always runs
steps.note: The line after `use` executes even when the test throws. This is the guarantee that leftover state cannot leak into the next test — the invariant made real.

steps.label: Skip the flaky UI login
steps.note: apiLogin sets the session cookie directly. The checkout test should test checkout, not re-run the login UI every time — the #1 place hard sleeps get added.

fixture-design.caption: Run it with `npx playwright test --trace=on`: the login step is gone from the trace, the flake rate drops to zero across 50 CI runs.

fixture-design.title: Two ways to give a test its user
fixture-design.subtitle: Same checkout suite. Both are green on your laptop. Only one survives CI.

left.label: Shared global fixture
lines: One seeded user for the whole suite
Login once, reuse storageState everywhere
State built through the UI in beforeAll
No teardown — cart persists between tests
A `waitForTimeout` patches the race
left.verdict: Passes locally, ~20% flake in CI — order-dependent

right.label: Scoped fixture with teardown
lines: Unique user seeded per test via API
Fresh authenticated context each test
State built through the backend, not the browser
Teardown after `use` runs pass or fail
No sleeps — determinism removed the race
right.verdict: Identical local + CI; 0 flake across 50 runs

fixture-design.caption: The tell: the weak version's result depends on which test ran first. A fixture you cannot run in isolation is not isolated.

fixture-design.text: The senior move is to pick fixture scope by the isolation-vs-cost tradeoff on purpose. Worker-scoped for expensive, read-only base state (a migrated DB); test-scoped for anything the test mutates (users, carts, sessions). The flake almost always lives where mutable state was made worker-scoped to 'go faster.' Speed you cannot trust is not speed.

fixture-design.question: A reviewer challenges your fixture design: "Prove this actually removed the flake, don't just tell me it's cleaner." Which response is real evidence?
options: The code reads more clearly and follows Playwright's fixture pattern.
50 CI runs of the checkout suite at 0 failures, plus a --trace=on capture of a pre-fix failure showing the shared-cart leak, attached to the packet.
The test passes locally every time I run it.
I added retries: 2 in the config so intermittent failures pass on rerun.
fixture-design.explanation: Only option 2 is operational proof: it replays the original failure (the trace showing the leak) and demonstrates the repair under CI conditions (50 clean runs). Cleaner code (1) and local passing (3) are exactly the false confidence the lesson targets. Retries (4) hide flake instead of removing it — the failure is still there, just masked.

fixture-design.intro: Prove the fixture design holds — no vibes:
items: Run one test in isolation with `npx playwright test path/to.spec.ts`. If it only passes as part of the full suite, it depends on state a sibling created — it is not isolated.
Grep the spec for `waitForTimeout` / hard sleeps. Each one is a fixture problem in disguise; a scoped fixture should let you delete it.
Confirm every fixture that mutates state has a teardown AFTER `use` — and force a failure mid-test to prove teardown still runs.
Run the suite with `--trace=on` and open `npx playwright show-report`: the trace of the previously flaky step should now be deterministic.
Run the suite 20–50 times in CI (or `--repeat-each`). A design that removes flake shows a flat 0-failure line, not 'mostly green.'

prompts: Explain to a teammate why 'passes locally, fails in CI' is almost always a fixture-scope problem, not a timing problem — using your own suite as the example.
In your own words: what is the difference between worker-scoped and test-scoped fixture state, and which one did your flaky test get wrong?
Why is a guaranteed teardown the thing that makes isolation real, and what breaks if teardown only runs on the happy path?

fixture-design.text: Fixture design is not a Playwright trick — it is the discipline of controlling the world a test starts from, and it travels. A pytest suite that shares a database session flakes for the identical reason; the fix is the same scoped-fixture-plus-teardown move. Now change the environment: in a regulated enterprise flow you cannot seed real PII, so the fixture provisions synthetic users behind a data-masking boundary; at high scale you make expensive base state worker-scoped and isolate only what mutates. What stays invariant across every one of them: no test may depend on state another test left behind. Carry the packet you built into the capstone — the CI quality gate reuses this exact flake-repair artifact as its proof that the release is safe to ship.

test-data-isolation.outcome: Take one flaky Playwright suite (yours or a realistic one) and prove its flake is a shared-state problem: name the shared fixture two tests fight over, isolate each test's data with a unique seed, and show the run go green under parallel workers. Package the decision as sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md.
test-data-isolation.proof: sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md with: the constraint, the selected isolation approach, the rejected approach, the exact failure trigger, the Playwright trace/screenshot proving the repair, and a CI gate result. A reviewer can replay the flaky run, see the shared row two tests collided on, then see it green after isolation.
test-data-isolation.unlock: Your packet names the shared-state collision, isolates per-test data with a unique key, and shows the same suite green under --workers>1 with a trace as evidence.
test-data-isolation.doNotClaim: Do not claim 'the test is isolated' because it passes on your laptop. A test that passes serially at --workers=1 but fails at --workers=4 is NOT isolated — it is just alone. Isolation is proven under parallelism against a shared store, or it is not proven.

test-data-isolation.text: Release is blocked: the checkout suite is green locally and red in CI, so nobody trusts it and the flaky tests get retried until they pass — which is the same as having no tests at all. The real culprit isn't timing; it's two tests both editing user 'testuser@acme.com' and stepping on each other.

In Automation Foundations the recurring failure is 'passes locally, fails in CI' — and the deepest cause under that umbrella is shared test data. Isolation is Section-worthy because a release decision made on a suite that fights over its own fixtures is a decision made on noise.

test-data-isolation.prompt: Your login test seeds a user 'qa_user', asserts, and passes every time you run it alone. In CI it fails ~1 run in 5. Same code, same assertions. Before reading on: what changed between 'alone' and 'CI'?
test-data-isolation.reveal: Concurrency changed. Locally you run one test at a time; CI runs workers in parallel. A second test also uses 'qa_user' — it deletes or mutates the row mid-flight, so your assertion hits state you didn't create. The flake isn't random and it isn't timing: it's a shared row two tests race on. 'Passes alone' is the tell of missing isolation, not the proof of a good test.

test-data-isolation.title: Isolation = each test owns data no other test can touch
test-data-isolation.text: Give every test its own uniquely-keyed data (run-id + worker + test name), never a shared fixture. The invariant: any test can run in any order, at any worker count, and still sees only what it created. Shared state is the flake.

test-data-isolation.title: Where shared test data becomes a flake
test-data-isolation.subtitle: Two parallel Playwright workers both seed and assert against the SAME user row. The collision on the shared store (red) is the flake source; the fix is a per-test namespace so each worker owns a distinct row.

legend.label: shared state = the collision = the flake

test-data-isolation.caption: The flake lives on the shared-row edge, not in the assertions. Isolation removes that edge by giving each worker its own key.

test-data-isolation.title: The isolation fixture, built line by line
test-data-isolation.subtitle: A Playwright worker-scoped fixture that seeds a UNIQUE user per test and tears it down — so no two tests can collide on the same row.

steps.label: Worker-scoped fixture
steps.note: Playwright gives each test its own `user`. testInfo carries workerIndex + title — the raw material for a collision-proof key.

steps.label: The unique key
steps.note: workerIndex separates parallel workers; Date.now() separates reruns; title separates tests on the same worker. This is the whole isolation move.

steps.label: Seed unique data
steps.note: Each test creates its OWN user via the API. No shared 'qa_user' row exists to race on.

steps.label: Hand off, then reclaim
steps.note: `use()` runs the test with the isolated user; the line after is teardown — always delete, so a crashed run doesn't poison the next.

steps.label: Teardown is not optional
steps.note: Skipping deleteUser is how 'isolated' suites slowly rot: residue accumulates until an unrelated test trips on it weeks later.

test-data-isolation.caption: Run this at --workers=4: every test seeds qa+<worker>-<time>-<title>@example.test. There is no shared row left to collide on.

test-data-isolation.title: Shared fixture vs isolated fixture
test-data-isolation.subtitle: Same login suite, same assertions. One passes only when alone; one passes at any worker count.

left.label: Shared 'qa_user' fixture
lines: beforeAll seeds one user 'qa_user'
3 specs all read/mutate that one row
Green at --workers=1 (serial, no race)
Red ~1-in-5 at --workers=4 in CI
Retry until green -> tests prove nothing
No teardown: residue leaks across runs
left.verdict: Passes alone, not isolated — flake blocks release

right.label: Per-test isolated fixture
lines: Each test seeds qa+<worker>-<time>-<title>
No shared row exists to race on
Green at --workers=1 AND --workers=4
Order-independent: shuffle passes too
Teardown deletes each user after use
Trace shows the exact row each test owned
right.verdict: Order- and worker-independent — release-safe

test-data-isolation.caption: The tell isn't 'does it pass' — it's 'does it still pass at --workers=4 in random order'. Only the right column can answer yes.

test-data-isolation.text: The senior tell: an SDET never says 'the test is flaky' — they say 'these two tests share state, here's the row.' Flake is a symptom; shared data, order dependence, or a leaked fixture is the disease. Run `npx playwright test --workers=4 --repeat-each=5` and watch which specs only fail together — collisions travel in pairs.

test-data-isolation.question: A reviewer challenges: 'You isolated the DB user, but your suite still fails ~1 run in 10 at --workers=4.' What is the most likely remaining shared-state leak?
options: The assertions are too strict and should be loosened until it's green.
A shared resource OTHER than the user row — a global browser storageState, a fixed port, a shared file/upload path, or a hard-coded record ID two tests still both touch.
CI is simply slower than local, so add a longer timeout everywhere.
Parallel workers are unsafe; drop back to --workers=1 permanently.
test-data-isolation.explanation: Isolating the user row removes ONE shared edge, not all of them. The next collision is usually another shared artifact — a reused storageState auth file, a fixed upload filename, a hard-coded 'order #1001', or a singleton test account. Loosening assertions (0) hides the bug; blanket timeouts (2) treat a race as latency; --workers=1 (3) masks the defect by removing the pressure that exposes it. Find the next shared thing and give each test its own.

test-data-isolation.intro: Prove isolation — no vibes, the packet must show each:
items: The suite passes at --workers=4 AND in shuffled order, not just at --workers=1. Run both; paste both results.
Every test's seeded data carries a unique key (worker + run-id + test). Grep the fixture: no hard-coded shared email/ID remains.
Teardown runs even on failure — a crashed test leaves no residue. Confirm the delete is after `use()`, not gated behind a passing assertion.
Attach a Playwright trace (`--trace=on`) that shows the exact isolated row this test owned — the reviewer can replay it.
The CI gate is green on a clean run with zero retries. A green that needed `--retries` is not proof of isolation; it's proof of a hidden flake.

prompts: In your own words: why does 'passes at --workers=1' actively HIDE the bug instead of proving the test is good?
Explain the unique key (worker + run-id + title) to a junior — what collision does each part of it prevent?
Your suite is isolated on the DB user but still flakes 1-in-10. Walk through how you'd hunt the next shared resource without loosening a single assertion.

test-data-isolation.text: Isolation is not a Playwright trick — it's the law for any parallel system that shares state. A pytest suite gets it from per-test DB transactions rolled back at teardown; a load test gets it from per-virtual-user accounts; a data pipeline gets it from partitioned scratch namespaces. Change the platform and the mechanism changes (transaction rollback vs unique-key seeding vs ephemeral schema) but the invariant is fixed: any unit can run in any order, at any concurrency, and see only what it created. Carry sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md into the capstone — the same constraint table, isolated fixture, and trace evidence become your flake-triage proof that a release gate can actually trust.

user-visible-behavior-tests.outcome: Take one revenue-critical web flow whose release is blocked by a flaky browser test, and write a decision packet that pins the user-visible assertion, names the flake's real cause, and proves the repair with a Playwright trace — not a re-run.
user-visible-behavior-tests.proof: sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md: the user-visible behavior under test (what the customer sees, not an internal state), the flake autopsy (selector | timing | fixture | environment), the chosen locator + web-first assertion, the Playwright trace/screenshot showing green, and the CI gate decision (ship | block). A reviewer can replay the trace and agree the flake is dead, not muted.
user-visible-behavior-tests.unlock: Your packet names the user-visible assertion, classifies the flake by cause, and attaches trace evidence that the repair holds under CI conditions — not just locally.
user-visible-behavior-tests.doNotClaim: Do not claim a test is 'fixed' because it passed on retry. A green re-run with retries: 2 and no root cause is a muted flake, not a repair. If you cannot point to the selector, wait, fixture, or env assumption you changed — and a trace that proves it — you hid the failure, you did not kill it.

user-visible-behavior-tests.text: Friday, 4 p.m.: the checkout release is one green check away, and that check has failed 3 of the last 10 CI runs on nobody's code change. Half the room says "just add retries and merge," the other half says "block it" — and neither has opened the trace to see what the browser actually did.

An end-to-end test earns its keep by asserting what the user sees — the confirmation, the price, the error toast — not an internal flag. This lesson turns a flaky, untrustworthy browser test into an inspectable release decision: the first section of the packet you carry through the module.

user-visible-behavior-tests.prompt: A checkout test does `await page.waitForTimeout(3000)` then checks the total. It passes locally, fails ~30% in CI. Before you touch the timeout — what is actually wrong? Answer before reading on.
user-visible-behavior-tests.reveal: The `sleep` is the bug, not the timeout value. `waitForTimeout` asserts nothing — it races the app against a fixed clock, and CI's slower, shared runner loses that race a third of the time. The fix is not 5000ms; it is deleting the sleep and letting a web-first assertion (`await expect(total).toHaveText('$42.00')`) auto-wait for the real user-visible state. A test that waits on a clock tests your guess about timing; a test that waits on a condition tests the product.

user-visible-behavior-tests.title: Assert user-visible state with an auto-waiting locator — never a sleep
user-visible-behavior-tests.text: A user-visible behavior test drives the app like a customer and asserts what the customer sees, through a role-based locator and a web-first assertion that auto-retries until the condition is true or times out. No fixed sleeps, no internal state, no brittle CSS paths.

user-visible-behavior-tests.title: Flake triage: same red test, four causes, four repairs
user-visible-behavior-tests.subtitle: A CI failure enters at the top; the decision tree routes it to a cause class and its repair. Only a confirmed cause + green trace reaches the release gate — a bare re-run loops back to the muted-flake trap.

legend.label: the muted-flake trap (retries, no root cause)

user-visible-behavior-tests.title: The repaired user-visible test, line by line
user-visible-behavior-tests.subtitle: The weak version raced a sleep against a brittle CSS path; the gold version asserts what the customer sees, auto-waiting on a role locator.

steps.label: Locate by role + name, not CSS
steps.note: getByRole mirrors what a screen reader and a user perceive. A `.btn-primary.checkout--v2` path breaks the next time design ships; the accessible name 'Checkout' is stable because it IS the user-visible contract.

steps.label: Assert with a web-first assertion
steps.note: expect(...).toHaveText auto-retries until the total renders or the timeout hits. This is what replaces the deleted waitForTimeout — the test waits on the condition, not a guessed clock, so the CI timing race disappears.

steps.label: Assert the user-visible value
steps.note: '$42.00' is what the customer reads on screen. Asserting the DOM total (not a computed variable in app state) is the whole point of a user-visible behavior test.

steps.label: Prove the outcome, not the plumbing
steps.note: A visible 'Order confirmed' heading is the behavior the business cares about. Checking an internal isPaid boolean would pass even if the confirmation never rendered — a green test hiding a broken flow.

user-visible-behavior-tests.caption: Run with `npx playwright test --trace=on`; open `npx playwright show-report`. The trace shows the click, the auto-wait resolving, and the confirmation — the repair, replayable by any reviewer.

user-visible-behavior-tests.title: Two checkout tests, one release decision
user-visible-behavior-tests.subtitle: Both are 'green on my machine.' Only one survives CI and tells you why.

left.label: Weak: brittle + racy
lines: await page.click('.btn-primary.checkout--v2')
await page.waitForTimeout(3000)  // guess
expect(await store.getState().isPaid).toBe(true)
Asserts internal state, not what the user sees
Fails ~30% in CI; 'fixed' with retries: 2
left.verdict: Passes locally, muted in CI — false confidence

right.label: Gold: user-visible + auto-waiting
lines: getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout' }).click()
await expect(total).toHaveText('$42.00')  // auto-wait
await expect(confirmHeading).toBeVisible()
Asserts what the customer actually reads
Deterministic in CI; trace proves each step
right.verdict: Green because the flow works — replayable proof

user-visible-behavior-tests.caption: The gold test would still catch a real regression (wrong total, missing confirmation); the weak test passes even when the customer sees nothing. Retries mute the symptom; the role locator + web-first assertion remove the cause.

user-visible-behavior-tests.text: The senior tell in flake triage: they open the trace before they re-run. A re-run that goes green tells you the failure is intermittent — which you already knew. The trace's DOM snapshot and network timeline tell you WHY: the element wasn't attached yet, the fixture bled state, the CI locale rendered '42,00' not '42.00'. `retries` is a shock absorber for a car you refuse to look under the hood of.

user-visible-behavior-tests.question: A browser test passes locally but fails ~1 in 4 CI runs. Which response is the SDET move that unblocks the release with proof?
options: Set `retries: 3` in the Playwright config so CI goes green, then merge.
Open the trace, classify the cause (selector / timing / fixture / env), fix the root cause, and attach the green trace to the release decision.
Mark the test `test.skip` and file a ticket to look at it later.
Increase every `waitForTimeout` in the suite from 3000ms to 8000ms.
user-visible-behavior-tests.explanation: Only option 2 produces a release decision a reviewer can inspect: a named cause and a replayable trace proving the repair. Retries (1) and longer sleeps (4) mute the symptom while the flake — and its false confidence — survive into production. Skipping (3) deletes coverage on a revenue-critical flow, which is worse than a flake: now nothing guards checkout.

user-visible-behavior-tests.intro: Prove the packet holds — trace evidence, not vibes:
items: Your assertion checks a user-visible value (rendered text, a visible heading, an error toast) — not an internal store flag or a network 200. If it would pass with a blank screen, it is not a behavior test.
Every wait is a web-first assertion or an explicit locator wait — grep the test for `waitForTimeout`; a fixed sleep left in is an unproven timing guess.
Locators are role- or testid-based, not CSS/xpath tied to styling. Ask: would this break when design renames a class? If yes, re-anchor it.
The flake is classified: you wrote down selector | timing | fixture | env and the ONE cause the trace confirmed — not a shrug.
You ran `--trace=on` and can open `show-report` to replay the green run. The trace is attached to the packet as the proof the gate reads.
The fixture seeds its own state per test (no reliance on run order or leftover data), so the pass is not an accident of what ran before it.

prompts: In your own words: why does asserting an internal `isPaid` flag give false confidence that a user-visible `toBeVisible()` on the confirmation heading does not?
Explain the difference between muting a flake (retries) and repairing it (root cause + trace), using the exact cause you found in your own packet.
Which cause class was your flake — selector, timing, fixture, or env — and what in the Playwright trace let you rule out the other three?

user-visible-behavior-tests.text: The move travels past checkout and past Playwright: assert what the user perceives, wait on conditions not clocks, and let a replayable artifact — not a re-run — carry the release decision. In a stricter env it tightens: a regulated enterprise flow adds an accessibility check to the same gate (the confirmation must be announced to a screen reader, not just visible), and a high-scale product shards the suite across CI so fixture isolation stops being polite and becomes mandatory. Same packet, higher bar. Next module reuses this exact `sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md` as your capstone evidence: not "I understand E2E testing" but "here is a flaky release I triaged, repaired, and proved green — replay the trace."

locator-strategy.outcome: Take one real (or realistic) flaky Playwright test and rewrite its locators by resilience tier — user-facing role/label first, test-id second, CSS/XPath last — then write the locator_strategy_decision_packet.md: the constraint, the selected tier per element, the rejected selector, and the exact failure each brittle locator would throw in CI.
locator-strategy.proof: locator_strategy_decision_packet.md with a constraint table, per-element selected tier, one rejected selector, the CI failure it causes, and two inspection-hook outputs (npx playwright test --trace=on + npx playwright show-report). A reviewer replays the trace and agrees each locator survives a class refactor and a re-render.
locator-strategy.unlock: Every locator in your test is chosen by tier with a stated reason, the rejected brittle option is recorded, and you can name the exact CI error each brittle selector would have thrown.
locator-strategy.doNotClaim: Do not claim a locator is 'stable' because it passes locally. Passing on your machine proves nothing about CI, where render timing, seeded data, and browser differ. Stability is a property you prove against a trace, not a green checkmark on your laptop.

locator-strategy.text: The release is blocked: getByCss('.btn-primary.sc-a3f9x') passed 200 times locally and now fails in CI on every run because a styled-components hash rotated overnight. A staff SDET opens one trace, points at the selector, and says the quiet part out loud — 'that test never located a button, it located a paint job.'

A selector is a bet on what stays stable while the app changes around it. Locator strategy is choosing bets that track how the user finds the element — its role and label — instead of how the framework happened to render it this build, which is the difference between a suite that survives refactors and one that flakes the release gate shut.

locator-strategy.prompt: Two selectors target the same submit button: page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }) and page.locator('div > form > button.sc-1x2y3z:nth-child(3)'). Both pass today. Which one is more likely to still pass after next sprint's redesign — and why? Decide before reading.
locator-strategy.reveal: The role+name one, and not because it's shorter. It binds to the accessible contract the user actually depends on — a button labelled 'Place order' — which a redesign is unlikely to change without changing the product. The nth-child/CSS-hash locator binds to DOM structure and a build-time class hash, both of which a redesign or even a Prettier reflow silently rewrites. The brittle one isn't 'less clean'; it's testing the markup instead of the behavior, so it breaks the moment the markup moves and the behavior doesn't.

locator-strategy.title: Locate by user contract, not by DOM accident
locator-strategy.text: Prefer the selector highest on the resilience tier: getByRole/getByLabel (the user-visible contract) → getByTestId (an explicit stable handle) → CSS/XPath (structure — brittle). The invariant: locate what the user perceives, never how the framework rendered it this build.

locator-strategy.title: The locator resilience hierarchy
locator-strategy.subtitle: Top tier binds to what the user perceives and survives refactors; the bottom tier binds to DOM structure and breaks when markup, class hashes, or timing shift. CI is where the bottom tier fails.
