locator-strategy.title: Rewriting a flaky test by tier
locator-strategy.subtitle: The same checkout test — before/after — plus the auto-wait that kills the sleep-based flake. Each step is a forcing function.

steps.label: The rejected selector
steps.note: CSS hash (.sc-a3f9x) rotates every build; :nth-child(3) shifts when a promo banner re-renders. In CI this throws 'locator resolved to 0 elements' or clicks the wrong node. Record it as the rejected option in the packet.

steps.label: The sleep that flakes
steps.note: waitForTimeout is a guess about render time. Faster CI passes, slower CI times out — the classic 'passes locally, fails in CI'. Delete it; never sleep to wait for the DOM.

steps.label: Tier 1 — role + name
steps.note: getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }) binds to the accessible contract the user depends on. A redesign that keeps the button labelled the same keeps this test green — and it doubles as an accessibility check: no accessible name, no locator.

steps.label: Tier 2 — testid, only when needed
steps.note: The total has no natural role/label, so an explicit data-testid is the honest choice — stable by decree, not by accident. Reach here second, never first.

steps.label: Auto-waiting assertions
steps.note: expect(...).toHaveText / toBeVisible retry until true or time out — this is the real flake fix. The locator says WHAT; the web-first assertion handles WHEN. Together they remove the timing race the sleep tried to paper over.

locator-strategy.caption: Run npx playwright test --trace=on, then npx playwright show-report: the trace shows each locator resolving to exactly one node — the proof a reviewer replays.

locator-strategy.title: Weak vs gold locator packet
locator-strategy.subtitle: Same button, same test. One describes a selector; one proves a strategy.

left.label: Weak: brittle by default
lines: page.locator('.btn-primary.sc-a3f9x:nth-child(3)')
Bound to a styled-components class hash + DOM index
waitForTimeout(2000) to 'let it settle'
No rejected option recorded, no failure predicted
Passes locally; in CI: 'locator resolved to 0 elements'
Tests the markup, not the behavior
left.verdict: Flakes the release gate shut on the next reflow

right.label: Gold: chosen by tier, proven by trace
lines: getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' })
Bound to the accessible name the user relies on
Auto-waiting expect(...).toBeVisible() — no sleep
Rejected .sc-a3f9x logged + its exact CI error named
Trace shows one node resolved; a11y name required to pass
Survives a class refactor AND a re-render
right.verdict: Green across refactors — a trustable gate

locator-strategy.caption: The gold column isn't 'cleaner code' — it's a bet on the user's contract instead of the build's markup, with the losing bet written down so a reviewer can challenge it.

locator-strategy.text: The senior tell: locator strategy IS accessibility strategy. getByRole only works if the element has a real role and accessible name — so a suite locked to Tier 1 fails loudly on inaccessible markup, turning your flake budget and your a11y conformance into the same fight. Playwright's own guidance ranks user-facing locators first for exactly this reason: the test that finds the element the way a screen reader does is the test that survives redesigns.

locator-strategy.question: A reviewer challenges: 'You used getByTestId('submit-btn') on a button that renders visible text "Place order". Defend it or fix it.' What's the correct response?
options: Keep the testid — data-testid is always the most stable option, so it's the right default.

Fix it: prefer getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }) — it binds to the user-facing contract, survives redesigns AND verifies the button is accessible; reserve testid for elements with no natural role/label.
Keep the testid and also add an nth-child fallback for safety.
Switch to XPath so the selector is fully explicit about DOM position.
locator-strategy.explanation: Test-id is a resilient handle, but it's tier 2 — a fallback for elements with no natural accessible name, not a default. A button with visible text 'Place order' already exposes a role and accessible name, so getByRole is strictly better: same resilience to structural change, plus it fails when the button loses its accessible name (catching a real a11y regression). Reaching for testid first (1), stacking a brittle fallback (3), or dropping to XPath (4) all trade away signal for false safety.

locator-strategy.intro: Prove your locators hold — no vibes, replay the trace:
items: For every locator, name its tier (role/label · testid · CSS/XPath) and why the tier above it wasn't available. If any Tier-3 CSS/XPath selector has no defense for skipping Tier 1 and 2, rewrite it.
Grep the test for waitForTimeout / sleep. Any fixed sleep is a latent CI flake — replace it with a web-first assertion (toBeVisible / toHaveText) that auto-waits.
Run npx playwright test --trace=on and open npx playwright show-report: confirm each locator resolves to exactly ONE element, not zero and not many (strict-mode violation).

For each brittle selector you rejected, write the exact CI error it would throw ('resolved to 0 elements' on a hash rotation, or a wrong-node click on a re-render). If you can't name the failure, you haven't proven the risk.
Confirm your Tier-1 locators would still pass a class-name refactor and a component re-render — the two changes that break structural selectors — by reasoning through each against the trace.

prompts: In your own words: why does a selector bound to a CSS class hash pass locally for weeks and then fail on every CI run at once?
Explain the resilience hierarchy to a junior using one element from your own test — why role/label beat testid, and why testid beat CSS here.
Your test uses getByRole. Explain how that single choice also protects accessibility, and what would make the locator fail in a way that's actually a real bug worth catching.

locator-strategy.text: The move is universal: locate by the stable contract, not the volatile representation. A mobile SDET picks accessibility IDs over view-hierarchy indices; an API test asserts on the response contract, not field order; a data pipeline keys on a business ID, not a row position. Anywhere a test binds to something the system is free to change without changing behavior, it will flake — and the fix is always to re-anchor onto what the user or the contract actually guarantees. You've now got Section 1 of the SDET quality-gate packet: carry locator_strategy_decision_packet.md into flake triage, where the same trace you captured here becomes the evidence that a failure is a real regression and not a brittle selector — the difference between a CI gate that blocks bad releases and one that blocks all of them.

auto-waiting-and-flake-reduction.outcome: Take one flaky browser test that blocks a revenue-critical release and repair it: replace the timing hack with a web-first assertion on the exact user-visible state, then produce a decision packet that names the constraint, the rejected fix, and the trace proof.
auto-waiting-and-flake-reduction.proof: sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md with a constraint table, the selected auto-waiting fix, the rejected sleep-based fix, the exact flake trigger, and one Playwright trace/screenshot showing the assertion passing on the retried state. A reviewer can replay the failure and the repair.
auto-waiting-and-flake-reduction.unlock: Your packet shows a web-first locator + assertion (no fixed sleep), names the flake class it removes, and attaches trace evidence a reviewer can inspect.
auto-waiting-and-flake-reduction.doNotClaim: Do not claim a test is 'de-flaked' because it passed once locally. A green local run is the flake's disguise, not its cure. The proof is a CI-reproducible trace showing the assertion auto-waited for the real condition, not that you got lucky on timing.

auto-waiting-and-flake-reduction.text: The checkout release is frozen: the browser suite is green on your laptop and red one run in five in CI, and nobody trusts the pipeline anymore. A staff SDET opens the trace, points at one line, and says the test never waited for the button to be actionable, it waited for a number someone guessed.

This is lesson 3 of End-To-End And Browser Automation: you already write Playwright specs with locators and assertions, now you make them survive CI. Flake is the tax on operational trust, and auto-waiting is how you stop paying it without arbitrary sleeps.

auto-waiting-and-flake-reduction.prompt: A test fails intermittently, so a teammate adds `await page.waitForTimeout(2000)` before the click and it 'fixes' it. Before you approve the PR, what did that actually do? Answer first.
auto-waiting-and-flake-reduction.reveal: It hid the flake and added two seconds of new flake. A fixed timeout races the app: 2s is too long on a fast CI node (slow suite) and too short on a loaded one (still flaky). Playwright's locators already auto-wait for an element to be attached, visible, stable, and actionable before acting, and web-first assertions like expect(locator).toBeVisible() retry until true or timeout. The sleep opts OUT of that machinery and replaces a real condition with a guess about the clock.

auto-waiting-and-flake-reduction.title: Auto-waiting: assert the condition, never the clock
auto-waiting-and-flake-reduction.text: Playwright actions and web-first assertions poll for the real user-visible state (visible, stable, enabled) until it holds or the timeout fires. Flake reduction = express the exact condition, delete every fixed sleep.

auto-waiting-and-flake-reduction.title: Where a browser test flakes, and where auto-waiting removes it
auto-waiting-and-flake-reduction.subtitle: The checkout flow: the test acts against a moving app. A fixed sleep bets on timing; a web-first assertion polls the real state until it holds or the timeout box fires.

nodes.label: Trace evidence
nodes.description: replayable proof of the retried state

auto-waiting-and-flake-reduction.title: Repairing the flaky checkout test, line by line
auto-waiting-and-flake-reduction.subtitle: The real Build artifact: brittle CSS + sleep + generic wait replaced with a role locator and a web-first assertion, plus the trace flags that prove it.

steps.label: The two flake sources
steps.note: A CSS-class selector breaks when styling changes, and waitForTimeout races the app. Both are commented out because both are the disease, not the cure.

steps.label: Role locator = auto-wait
steps.note: getByRole is a user-facing locator. Before the click, Playwright waits for the button to be attached, visible, stable (not animating), and enabled. No sleep needed.

steps.label: Assert the condition, not the clock
steps.note: toContainText retries until the status region actually says 'Order confirmed' or the assertion timeout fires. This is the exact user-visible post-state, so it cannot pass early.

steps.label: Pin the outcome, not the render
steps.note: toHaveURL confirms navigation to a real receipt id. Two independent post-conditions make a false green far less likely.

steps.label: Prove it in CI, not on your laptop
steps.note: Run `npx playwright test --trace=on` then `npx playwright show-report`; attach the trace. Set retries:2 in config so a genuine flake is quarantined and surfaced, never silently passed.

auto-waiting-and-flake-reduction.caption: Run `npx playwright test --project=chromium --trace=on`; open the trace and confirm the assertion step shows a retry that resolved on the confirmed state, not a fixed delay.

auto-waiting-and-flake-reduction.title: Two fixes for the same flaky test
auto-waiting-and-flake-reduction.subtitle: Incident: 'checkout test fails ~1 in 5 in CI.' Both make it green today. Only one removes the flake class and proves it.

left.label: Sleep-and-pray
lines: await page.click('.btn-primary')
await page.waitForTimeout(2000)
Waits on the clock, not the condition
Passes locally, still races under CI load
No trace, no named flake class, no stop rule
Reviewer cannot replay why it failed
left.verdict: Hides the flake, adds new timing risk

right.label: Web-first + evidence
lines: getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }).click()
expect(getByRole('status')).toContainText('Order confirmed')
Auto-waits for actionable + polls the real post-state
retries:2 quarantines genuine flakes instead of masking
--trace=on attaches a replayable proof
Packet names the flake class removed (timing race)
right.verdict: Removes the race and proves it in CI

auto-waiting-and-flake-reduction.caption: The gold fix asserts the condition (order confirmed), not the clock (2000ms). The trace is what turns 'it passes' into inspectable evidence a reviewer trusts.

auto-waiting-and-flake-reduction.text: The senior tell: never assert on a timer, and never assert on nothing. waitForTimeout is a code smell in a browser suite; a bare click with no follow-up assertion is worse. Every action should be followed by a web-first assertion on the state that action was supposed to produce, so a false green becomes structurally hard. When a flake survives that, quarantine it with retries and a trace before it burns another release, don't @flaky-skip it into the dark.

auto-waiting-and-flake-reduction.question: A reviewer challenges your 'de-flaked' checkout test. Which single piece of evidence best proves the flake is actually gone rather than hidden?
options: The test passed ten times in a row on your local machine.
You replaced getByRole with a more specific CSS selector for the button.
A CI trace (--trace=on) showing the web-first assertion auto-waited and resolved on the real confirmed-order state, with retries configured to surface any residual flake.
You increased waitForTimeout from 2000ms to 5000ms so it has more slack.
auto-waiting-and-flake-reduction.explanation: Only option 3 is inspectable operational proof under the environment that flakes (CI), tied to the real condition. Local reruns (1) don't reproduce CI load. A CSS selector (2) is more brittle, not less. A longer sleep (4) still asserts on the clock and just makes the suite slower while the race remains.

auto-waiting-and-flake-reduction.intro: Prove the repair holds, no vibes:
items: Grep the spec for waitForTimeout and fixed sleeps. If any remain on the suspect path, the flake class is not removed, delete them.
Every action is followed by a web-first assertion (expect(locator).toBeVisible/toContainText/toHaveURL) on the exact user-visible post-state that action produces.
Locators are user-facing (getByRole/getByLabel/getByText), not styling-coupled CSS classes that drift.
You ran `npx playwright test --trace=on` and can open the trace in `show-report` to point at the assertion step that auto-waited and resolved.
Config sets retries so a genuine flake is quarantined and reported, not silently passed, and your packet names the flake class (timing race / brittle selector / stale fixture) you eliminated.

prompts: Explain to a teammate why waitForTimeout(2000) is both too long and too short at the same time, using your own checkout test as the example.
In your own words: what does a web-first assertion poll for, and why does that make a false green structurally hard?
Point to the exact line in your trace that proves the test waited for the confirmed-order condition and not for a fixed delay.

auto-waiting-and-flake-reduction.text: This move is not Playwright-specific, it is the whole discipline of testing an asynchronous system: assert the condition, never the clock. In a smaller team you inline it as a lint rule that bans waitForTimeout; in a regulated enterprise the trace becomes the audit artifact attached to the CI quality gate that authorizes the release; at high scale you shard the suite and let retries + quarantine keep the flake rate below your merge-blocking threshold. The invariant across all three: a green test must be backed by a replayable proof that it waited for the real state. Carry the same packet into the module capstone, where this de-flaked test becomes one line in the release's CI gate decision.

visual-regression.outcome: Take one revenue-critical web flow (checkout, signup, pricing page) and write the Visual Regression Baseline Packet: which regions you snapshot, which you MASK as dynamic, the diff threshold you chose and why, and the exact CI gate decision the diff drives — no hand-waving.
visual-regression.proof: sdet_visual_regression_baseline_packet.md with a locator-scoped snapshot target, an explicit mask list, a numbered maxDiffPixelRatio + its rationale, a failure trigger, a reviewer-objection response, and the CI gate result. A peer can look at a red diff and predict whether your gate blocks the release.
visual-regression.unlock: Your packet names the snapshot scope, the masked dynamic regions, the threshold with a reason, and the exact block/pass rule the diff feeds the CI gate.
visual-regression.doNotClaim: Do not claim 'visual regression is covered' because you called toHaveScreenshot() once. A full-page snapshot with no masks and a default threshold flags on every timestamp and font-render wobble — that is a flake generator, not a gate. Coverage is the mask list plus the threshold rationale, not the assertion.

visual-regression.text: The pricing page ships. Nobody notices the CTA button turned the same color as the background until conversion craters over the weekend — every unit test was green, because not one of them can see. Visual regression is the only test that looks at the pixels a customer actually looks at.

This is lesson 4 of End-To-End And Browser Automation: you already framed the flow, wrote resilient locators, and stabilized timing. Visual regression adds the one signal those miss — an unintended pixel change — but only if you separate real regressions from dynamic noise, or it becomes the flakiest gate you own.

visual-regression.prompt: Your visual test snapshots the whole page and passes locally every time. In CI it fails on the very first run. Nothing about the UI changed. What broke? Answer before reading on.
visual-regression.reveal: The environment did. CI renders on a different OS with different font-hinting and antialiasing than your Mac, so millions of subpixels differ — a full-page, zero-tolerance snapshot flags all of it. The fix is not 'accept the new baseline'; it is to generate baselines IN CI (the same runner image), scope the snapshot to a locator, mask dynamic regions, and set maxDiffPixelRatio above the antialiasing floor. 'Passes locally, fails in CI' is the signature failure of this whole module — here it wears a visual mask.

visual-regression.title: A visual test = scoped snapshot + masked dynamics + a threshold you can defend
visual-regression.text: Snapshot the smallest region that holds the risk, mask everything non-deterministic (dates, avatars, ads), and set a diff threshold above the render-noise floor. The diff then means one thing: an unintended change a human should approve or block.

visual-regression.title: The visual regression pipeline — baseline, compare, gate
visual-regression.subtitle: A PR renders the flow, Playwright compares the fresh screenshot against the committed baseline, and the pixel-diff ratio drives the CI gate. Masked regions and the threshold are what keep the gate signal, not noise.

legend.label: diff + gate — intended vs unintended change

visual-regression.title: The visual test + its config, line by line
visual-regression.subtitle: The real Playwright artifact from the Build step — locator-scoped, masked, thresholded, animations frozen.

steps.label: Wait for a real anchor, not a timer
steps.note: Snapshot only after a deterministic element is present. A sleep() screenshots mid-render and produces a flaky baseline — the timing lesson, applied to pixels.

steps.label: Scope to a locator, not the page
steps.note: getByTestId('order-summary') snapshots one component. Full-page shots drown a real regression in unrelated layout churn and are the top source of visual flake.

steps.label: Mask the non-deterministic regions
steps.note: The order date and rotating promo banner change every run. Masking paints them a solid color in BOTH images so they can never trip the diff — this is the core skill.

steps.label: Set the threshold above the noise floor
steps.note: maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01 tolerates ~1% antialiasing/font-hinting jitter across runners. Zero tolerance flags render noise; too loose hides real regressions. Defend the number.

steps.label: Freeze animations
steps.note: animations: 'disabled' halts CSS transitions so the shot is deterministic. A spinner mid-frame is a different picture every run.

steps.label: Baselines are per-platform and CI-generated
steps.note: The golden is order-summary-chromium-linux.png, regenerated with --update-snapshots on the CI image. Committing a Mac baseline and comparing on Linux is exactly the pretest failure.

visual-regression.caption: Run it: change the CTA color and the diff.png lights up the button in magenta; the gate blocks. Move the masked date and nothing trips — signal, not noise.

visual-regression.title: Two visual suites, same flow
visual-regression.subtitle: Both call toHaveScreenshot(). Only one produces a diff a reviewer can trust.

left.label: Naive snapshot
lines: await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot() — whole page
No mask: date, avatar, ad rotate every run
Default zero-tolerance threshold
Baseline captured on a Mac, compared on Linux CI
Animations live; screenshot mid-transition
left.verdict: Red on every run — team disables it in a week

right.label: Engineered baseline
lines: Scoped to getByTestId('order-summary')
Dynamic regions masked in both images
maxDiffPixelRatio 0.01, chosen above the noise floor
Baseline generated in CI (same runner image)
animations: 'disabled', waits on a real anchor
right.verdict: Red means a human changed pixels on purpose — or didn't

visual-regression.caption: A visual gate is only worth its cost if a red diff is a decision, not a coin flip. The mask list and threshold rationale are what buy that trust.

visual-regression.text: Standards grounding: a visual diff is evidence, not a verdict. Every failing toHaveScreenshot leaves an expected/actual/diff triptych in test-results/ — attach it to the defect report and the CI gate decision. A senior SDET never auto-approves a new baseline with --update-snapshots without eyeballing the diff, because that command silently blesses whatever changed, including the regression you were trying to catch.

visual-regression.question: A reviewer challenges: 'Your visual test went red on a PR that only changed backend copy — prove this is a real regression and not flake.' What is the strongest response?
options: Re-run the job; if it passes the second time it was flake, so merge.
Open the diff.png artifact: it highlights the CTA button region, not the copy — the change shifted layout and moved the button, which the masked, locator-scoped snapshot caught deterministically.
Lower maxDiffPixelRatio to 0 so the test is stricter and more trustworthy.
Delete the baseline and regenerate it with --update-snapshots so the test is green again.
visual-regression.explanation: The diff artifact IS the proof: it shows exactly which pixels moved. Because the snapshot is scoped and dynamic regions are masked, a red diff can only mean an unintended visual change — here, a copy change that reflowed layout. Re-running (1) hides signal, tightening to 0 (3) manufactures flake, and blind --update-snapshots (4) blesses the regression.

visual-regression.intro: Prove your baseline packet holds — no vibes:
items: Run the suite twice with zero code changes. If any snapshot goes red, you have masking or threshold debt — a stable UI must diff clean on repeat.
List every masked region and name why each is non-deterministic (timestamp, user avatar, rotating ad). An unexplained mask is a hidden hole in coverage.
State your maxDiffPixelRatio and the noise floor it clears — confirm baselines were generated on the SAME runner image CI compares against, not your laptop.
Introduce a deliberate regression (recolor a button) and confirm the diff.png localizes it and the gate blocks. A visual gate that cannot fail proves nothing.
Confirm the CI gate rule is explicit: over-threshold diff → block + attach expected/actual/diff artifacts to the defect report, never a silent auto-update.

prompts: Explain to a junior why a full-page snapshot with no masks is the flakiest test on the suite — using a dynamic region from your own flow.
Why does 'passes locally, fails in CI' happen for visual tests specifically, and what two changes fix it?
Defend your maxDiffPixelRatio to a skeptic: what does it let through on purpose, and what would still trip it?

visual-regression.text: The same discipline scales by risk. On a small team, a handful of locator-scoped snapshots on the checkout and pricing pages beats a full-page suite nobody trusts. In a regulated enterprise, visual diffs become audit evidence — every baseline change reviewed and signed, dynamic-data masking mandatory for PII. At high scale, you shard visual tests across a browser grid and treat the baseline store as a versioned artifact. What stays invariant everywhere: scope the snapshot, mask the noise, defend the threshold, and make the diff a decision. This packet is your capstone evidence — a checkout flow you snapshotted, masked, thresholded, broke, and gated — reusable unchanged on the next revenue-critical page.

accessibility-checks.outcome: Take a revenue-critical web flow (real or realistic — a checkout, a sign-up, a search) and turn accessibility from a vibe into an automated CI quality gate. Wire an axe-core scan into a Playwright test that fails the build on serious/critical violations, then write the decision packet that proves the gate is real, not decorative.
accessibility-checks.proof: sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md with: the constraint, the selected approach (axe-core in Playwright, seriousness threshold, per-page scope), the rejected approach and why, the expected CI failure mode, the verification (a red build on an injected violation), a reviewer objection response, and the transfer case. Plus the committed accessibility.spec.ts that another engineer can run and read the trace from.
accessibility-checks.unlock: Your gate fails the build on a real serious/critical violation, passes clean, and the packet names the constraint, the rejected option, and one failure you can replay.
accessibility-checks.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have an 'accessibility gate' if the axe scan runs but its result never fails the pipeline — a check whose 'fail' is only logged is theater. And do not claim 'zero violations' from a scan that only touched the landing page; scope is part of the claim.

accessibility-checks.text: The release is one green checkmark from shipping when a screen-reader user files a ticket: the checkout's 'Place order' button is an unlabeled div, invisible to assistive tech, and it has been broken for three deploys. Every test passed. Nobody wrote the check that would have caught it.

This sits in Nonfunctional Quality Gates, where a release is blocked by flaky browser tests and untriaged accessibility defects. The question is boundary and ownership: does 'accessible' mean a human clicked around, or a machine-enforced gate a reviewer can inspect and replay?

accessibility-checks.prompt: Your team runs an axe-core accessibility scan in CI. It reports 12 violations on every run, the number never changes, and the build stays green. Is accessibility being tested? Answer before reading on.
accessibility-checks.reveal: No — it is being logged, not gated. A scan whose result cannot fail the pipeline is a dashboard nobody reads; the 12 violations are wallpaper. A real gate has a threshold (fail on serious/critical), a scope (which pages, which states), and teeth (a non-zero exit that blocks merge). Until 'fail' actually turns the build red, you have observability of accessibility, not a quality gate — and the two get confused precisely when it matters.

accessibility-checks.title: An accessibility gate is a scoped, thresholded check with teeth
accessibility-checks.text: Run an automated conformance scan (axe-core) inside a browser test, on named pages and states, asserting zero violations above a seriousness threshold. The assertion must be able to fail the CI build. Logged-but-green is not a gate — it is a report.

accessibility-checks.title: The accessibility gate on the release path
accessibility-checks.subtitle: Playwright drives the real checkout flow, axe-core scans each rendered state, the assertion converts serious/critical violations into a non-zero exit. The red path (build fails) and the repair path (fix, rescan, green) are both marked. Unit and contract tests are shown but out of scope for this gate.

legend.label: the gate's teeth — red build on serious/critical

accessibility-checks.title: The gate as a real Playwright + axe-core spec
accessibility-checks.subtitle: Scan the loaded page AND a mid-flow state, fail only on serious/critical, attach the report so the trace is inspectable.

steps.label: The threshold, named
steps.note: serious/critical block; minor/moderate are triaged, not gated. Naming it in code is the difference between a gate and an opinion — a reviewer can see exactly what fails the build.

steps.label: A role locator IS an a11y assertion
steps.note: getByRole reads the accessibility tree. If 'Place order' is an unlabeled div, this line fails before axe even runs. Prefer role/label locators over CSS selectors — they double as conformance checks and they do not rot when class names change.

steps.label: Scoped WCAG tags
steps.note: withTags pins the ruleset (WCAG 2.1 A + AA) so the gate is deterministic and defensible — 'which rules?' has a written answer, not 'whatever axe defaults to this version.'

steps.label: Scan a STATE, not just page load
steps.note: The landing render is the easy case. Violations breed in interactive states — the error banner with no aria-live, the modal that traps nothing. Scanning after the click is where this gate earns its keep.

steps.label: Filter to blocking impact
steps.note: This is the teeth. Only serious/critical survive into the assertion, so the build fails on real barriers, not on 100 cosmetic contrast notes that would train the team to ignore red.

steps.label: Attach the evidence
steps.note: testInfo.attach puts the exact violation report in the Playwright trace/HTML report — the proof a reviewer replays with `npx playwright show-report`. A gate with no attached evidence is a claim, not a check.

steps.label: The assertion with teeth
steps.note: expect(...).toEqual([]) returns a non-zero exit on failure, which fails the CI job. The custom message prints violation id + help so the red build is self-explaining, not a bare 'expected [] '.

accessibility-checks.caption: Run it: `npx playwright test --trace=on`. A green run proves scope + threshold; open `show-report` to read the attached axe report and the DOM node for any failure.

accessibility-checks.title: Two accessibility 'checks' on the same checkout
accessibility-checks.subtitle: Both appear in the pipeline. Only one can block a broken release.

left.label: Decorative scan
lines: axe runs once on the landing page only
Result is console.log'd, exit code always 0
No seriousness threshold — 40 mixed findings
No interactive state scanned (error/modal unchecked)
CSS-selector locators that pass on unlabeled divs
'We run accessibility checks' — technically true
left.verdict: Green while the flow is broken for AT users

right.label: Enforced gate
lines: axe on the checkout PAGE and its error STATE
expect(blocking).toEqual([]) → non-zero exit blocks merge
Threshold pinned: serious/critical only
WCAG 2.1 A+AA tags named in code
getByRole locators that fail on unlabeled controls
axe report attached to the Playwright trace
right.verdict: Red build the moment the button loses its label

accessibility-checks.caption: The tell is the exit code, the scope, and the threshold — not whether 'axe' appears in the logs. A check you cannot make fail on purpose has never been proven to work.

accessibility-checks.text: Standards grounding: automated tooling like axe-core catches roughly 30-40% of WCAG issues — missing labels, contrast, ARIA misuse, tab order violations it can infer. It cannot judge whether alt text is meaningful or whether focus order makes sense to a human. So the gate is a floor, not a ceiling: it blocks the regressions a machine can prove, and the packet must say so explicitly, or a reviewer will read 'axe passed' as 'accessible' — a claim the tool never made.

accessibility-checks.question: Reviewer challenge: your PR says 'accessibility gate added, checkout passes clean.' What single piece of evidence best proves the gate is real rather than decorative?
options: A screenshot of the axe-core scan reporting zero violations on the checkout page.
A CI run where a deliberately injected violation (e.g. an unlabeled button) turned the build RED, plus the attached axe report and the passing run after the fix.
A statement in the PR description that the team ran axe-core locally and it looked fine.
A green pipeline badge on the repository README.
accessibility-checks.explanation: A gate is only proven by a failure it can produce on demand. Injecting a real serious violation and showing the build go red — then green after repair — demonstrates threshold, scope, and teeth all at once. A passing screenshot (0), a verbal claim (2), and a green badge (3) are all consistent with a scan whose 'fail' is only logged; none of them show the check can block a broken release.

accessibility-checks.intro: Prove the gate holds — executable or it did not happen:
items: Inject one serious violation on purpose (remove an aria-label, or swap getByRole for a div) and run the spec. If the build does not go non-zero / red, your check has no teeth — it is a report.
Run `npx playwright test --trace=on` on the passing state, then `npx playwright show-report` and confirm the axe report is attached and the failing DOM node is findable in the trace.
Confirm the scan covers at least one INTERACTIVE state (post-click, error, or modal), not only the initial page load — name which states in the packet.
Confirm the seriousness threshold and WCAG tag set are written in the code, not implied. A reviewer should read 'serious/critical, WCAG 2.1 AA' without asking you.
Run the spec locally AND in CI. If it passes locally but errors in CI, name the cause (selector/timing/fixture/env) in the flake section before calling the gate stable.

prompts: In your own words: why is a role/label locator (getByRole) itself an accessibility assertion, and how does that make your test resist both flakiness and a11y regressions at once?
Explain the difference between an accessibility scan that is logged and one that is gated, using your own exit-code and threshold as the example.
axe-core covers ~30-40% of WCAG. Explain to a PM what your gate does guarantee and what it explicitly does not — and why claiming full accessibility from a green scan is a false-confidence failure.

accessibility-checks.text: The move is not 'accessibility' — it is turning any nonfunctional quality into a scoped, thresholded gate with teeth, and the same shape moves. On a smaller team: one axe gate on the single revenue flow, run on every PR, beats a quarterly manual audit nobody schedules. In a regulated enterprise (Section 508 / EN 301 549): the threshold tightens to zero serious AND documented triage of every moderate, and the attached report becomes an audit artifact. At high scale: you cannot scan every page, so you gate the top revenue flows and sample the long tail — scope becomes the design decision. Same skill applies to performance budgets, security headers, and contract tests: name the check, name the threshold, make 'fail' block the merge, attach the evidence. The `sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md` you built here is the reusable artifact — the capstone reuses it directly: the release gate that decides ship / no-ship is this same packet with the accessibility gate, the flake-triaged browser tests, and the CI decision joined into one inspectable record.

performance-smoke-tests.outcome: Take one revenue-critical web flow (checkout, login, add-to-cart) and write a performance smoke test that fails the CI gate on a p95 budget breach — plus the decision packet that names the constraint, the rejected option, and the exact failure it catches.
performance-smoke-tests.proof: sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md with: the flow under test, the p95 budget + why, the selected approach, the rejected approach, the expected failure, the verification method (Playwright trace + CI gate result), and one reviewer objection answered. A reviewer can replay the failure and the repair.
performance-smoke-tests.unlock: Your smoke test asserts a concrete latency/availability budget that can FAIL, runs in CI, and the packet names the constraint + rejected option + the exact failure it guards.
performance-smoke-tests.doNotClaim: Do not claim a 'performance smoke test' if it only checks the page eventually loads. A test with no budget threshold cannot fail on a regression — that is a page-load check wearing a performance costume. The threshold is the test.

performance-smoke-tests.text: Friday deploy, green pipeline, everyone goes home. Monday the funnel is down 8% and nobody can say when checkout got slow — because the tests only ever asked 'did it load?', never 'did it load in time?'

A performance smoke test is the fast, cheap release gate that runs one critical flow and fails the build when latency or availability crosses a budget. It sits between 'the feature works' and a full load test — the thin, blocking check that keeps a slow regression from ever reaching users.

performance-smoke-tests.prompt: Your smoke test navigates checkout and asserts the confirmation heading is visible. It passes locally and in CI. What performance regression can it never catch? Answer before reading on.
performance-smoke-tests.reveal: A slow one. `toBeVisible()` waits up to the default timeout (30s) and passes as long as the element eventually appears — so a checkout that degraded from 1.2s to 9s still goes green. A performance smoke test needs an explicit budget assertion (`expect(elapsed).toBeLessThan(2500)`) or it is measuring existence, not speed. The passing test is exactly what hides the regression.

performance-smoke-tests.title: A performance smoke test asserts a budget on one critical flow — fast, blocking, falsifiable
performance-smoke-tests.text: Drive one revenue-critical flow, measure a real latency signal (p95 of a key transition, or a Web Vital), and assert it against a budget the test can FAIL. Keep it fast enough to block every deploy. No threshold means no gate.

performance-smoke-tests.title: Where the performance smoke gate sits in the pipeline
performance-smoke-tests.subtitle: Checkout flow → measured p95 → budget decision. Green promotes; a breach blocks the deploy and drops a trace. Full load testing is deliberately downstream and out of the blocking path.

legend.label: the smoke gate — one flow, one budget

performance-smoke-tests.title: The smoke test that actually fails on a regression
performance-smoke-tests.subtitle: Playwright: drive checkout, measure the confirmation p95, assert the budget, attach a trace when it breaches.

steps.label: The budget IS the test
steps.note: A named threshold below the SLO with headroom. Without this constant there is nothing to fail — the whole gate hangs on this line.

steps.label: Drive the real revenue flow
steps.note: Role- and label-based locators, not brittle CSS/XPath — the flake-resistant choice that survives markup churn between local and CI.

steps.label: Measure the transition, don't just await it
steps.note: Time from 'Pay now' to the confirmation heading. Scoping the timeout to BUDGET_MS means a slow response fails via timeout, not a 30s default that quietly passes.

steps.label: Assert the budget with a message
steps.note: The falsifiable line: elapsed must beat the budget. The template message prints the real ms so a failure reads as a number, not 'timed out'.

performance-smoke-tests.caption: Run with --trace=on so every breach ships a replayable trace.zip; the CI job fails the deploy on a non-zero exit.

performance-smoke-tests.title: Existence check vs performance smoke test
performance-smoke-tests.subtitle: Same checkout flow, same Playwright API. Only one can fail when the flow gets slow.

left.label: Load check in a costume
lines: await expect(heading).toBeVisible()
Default 30s timeout — 9s checkout passes
No budget constant, no elapsed measure
CSS locator .btn-primary breaks in CI
Green build the day the funnel slowed
left.verdict: Measures existence — regression invisible

right.label: Real performance smoke test
lines: expect(elapsed).toBeLessThan(2500)
Budget below SLO with headroom
Times the Pay-now → confirmation transition
Role/label locators survive markup churn
Breach blocks deploy + attaches trace.zip
right.verdict: Falsifiable budget — regression fails the gate

performance-smoke-tests.caption: A test that can only pass is theater. The threshold is what turns a page-load check into a release gate.

performance-smoke-tests.text: The senior tell: budget on p95, not the mean, and set it BELOW your SLO. A mean hides the slow tail that actually loses conversions; a budget equal to the SLO gives zero warning — by the time it fails you are already breaching the promise. Leave headroom so the gate trips before customers feel it.

performance-smoke-tests.question: A reviewer says: 'This just proves checkout loads — how do I know it catches a slowdown?' What is the one change that answers them?
options: Add more steps to the flow so it exercises more of the app.
Replace the CSS locators with role-based locators to reduce flake.
Assert a measured latency against an explicit budget the test can fail (e.g. expect(elapsed).toBeLessThan(2500)).
Run the test on three browsers instead of one.
performance-smoke-tests.explanation: The reviewer's objection is exactly the pretest trap: a visibility check passes regardless of speed. Only an explicit budget assertion makes the test falsifiable on a regression. Better locators (2) reduce flake and more browsers (4) add coverage — both good, neither turns an existence check into a performance gate. The threshold does.

performance-smoke-tests.intro: Prove the gate is real — no vibes:
items: Break it on purpose: add an artificial 3s delay behind checkout and confirm the test FAILS. A gate that never goes red under a real slowdown is not a gate.
Confirm the assertion is a budget (elapsed < threshold), not just toBeVisible with a default timeout.
Run it twice in CI back-to-back — if it flips pass/fail with no code change, quarantine and fix the flake (locator or timing) before it guards a release.
Open the attached trace.zip in `npx playwright show-trace` and confirm you can see the slow transition, not just a stack trace.
Verify the CI job returns non-zero on breach so the deploy is actually blocked — a failing test that still promotes the build proves nothing.

prompts: In your own words: why does `toBeVisible()` with a default timeout let a performance regression pass, and what does the budget assertion change?
Explain why the smoke gate budgets p95 below the SLO instead of the mean at the SLO — use your own flow's numbers.
Walk a teammate through what happens to the pipeline, the trace, and the deploy when your budget is breached.

performance-smoke-tests.text: Same move, any surface with a budget and a clock. A backend team smoke-tests an API contract with a p95 response budget in the same gate; a mobile team asserts cold-start time before shipping a build; an SRE wires the identical threshold-on-a-critical-path pattern into a canary. What stays invariant is the discipline: one critical path, a falsifiable budget below the SLO, blocking, with a replayable trace on breach. What changes is the signal you measure and where the gate lives. This packet — the flow, the budget, the rejected option, the trace evidence — is the exact artifact your capstone reuses: not 'I understand performance gates' but 'here is a regression I made the pipeline catch, replay it.'

security-smoke-checks.outcome: Take one revenue-critical web flow (checkout, login, or account) and write a Security Smoke Check gate: a small, fast, deterministic suite that fails the release if an authz boundary, a security header, or a data-exposure invariant regresses. Then break it and prove the repair.
security-smoke-checks.proof: sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md with: the constraint, the selected approach, the rejected approach, the expected failure, the verification method (a Playwright/API run that returns a real pass/fail), a reviewer objection, and a transfer note. A reviewer can replay one check and watch it fail on an injected regression, then pass after repair.
security-smoke-checks.unlock: Your gate asserts at least one authz boundary, one security header, and one exposure invariant — each with a check that can return FAIL — and you have logged one failure trigger plus its repair.
security-smoke-checks.doNotClaim: Do not claim a 'security smoke check' if every assertion can only pass. A check that green-lights whether or not the app is safe is theater. Each assertion must be able to catch a real regression — anon hitting an authed route, a missing header, a token in a response body.

security-smoke-checks.text: The checkout release is green: 400 browser tests pass. It ships. Two hours later a customer opens someone else's order confirmation — the order API stopped checking ownership three commits ago, and not one test asked 'can an anonymous user reach this?' The suite proved the feature worked; nobody proved it was still locked.

Security smoke checks are a nonfunctional quality gate: a short, fast, deterministic band of tests that block a release when a security invariant regresses. They are not a pentest — they are the seatbelt light, the handful of assertions that must be true before any revenue flow ships.

security-smoke-checks.prompt: Your login and checkout E2E tests all pass. Does that tell you the flow is still secure? Answer before reading on.
security-smoke-checks.reveal: No — functional tests drive the app as an authorized, well-behaved user, so they exercise the happy path and never the boundary. 'Checkout works when I'm logged in' says nothing about whether checkout still refuses an anonymous request, still sets HSTS, or still keeps the CVV out of the response. Security lives on the paths your feature tests deliberately avoid. A smoke check is the opposite instinct: send the request the app should reject, and assert it gets rejected.

security-smoke-checks.title: A security smoke check is a fast, deterministic gate on a few must-hold invariants
security-smoke-checks.text: Pick the highest-risk invariants of a revenue flow — authz boundaries, security headers, no-secret-in-response — and assert each with a check that can FAIL. Keep it fast, deterministic, and release-blocking. It catches regressions, not novel exploits.

security-smoke-checks.title: Where the smoke check sits on the release path
security-smoke-checks.subtitle: Deploy → functional suite → the security smoke gate → release. The gate probes the authz boundary, headers, and response body; any FAIL blocks the release and the exposure branch never reaches production.

legend.label: the smoke gate and its three probes
release only when every invariant holds

security-smoke-checks.title: The gate, one assertion at a time
security-smoke-checks.subtitle: A Playwright security smoke spec for the checkout flow — three invariants, each able to FAIL.

steps.label: Deterministic target
steps.note: One fixed staging base URL from env — no ambient state, no random data. A smoke check that isn't deterministic becomes a flake, and a flaky gate gets disabled.

steps.label: Authz boundary — the FAIL path
steps.note: Send the request with NO auth cookie and assert it is rejected. If the ownership check regressed, status is 200 and the body carries line_items — this test goes red. That red is the whole point.

steps.label: Prove it wasn't a soft leak
steps.note: Status alone isn't enough: also assert the body did not return the protected payload. Some regressions return 200 with data even while a banner says 'unauthorized'.

steps.label: Header invariants
steps.note: Assert HSTS, nosniff, and CSP are present. A config change that drops a header passes every functional test and is invisible without this probe.

steps.label: Exposure invariant
steps.note: Authenticated as a real user, assert the response body has no raw card number and no secret field names. This catches a serializer that started over-returning fields.

steps.label: Trace evidence on failure
steps.note: Run under `--trace=on`; a red gate produces a replayable trace + request/response, so a reviewer sees the exact leaked payload, not a summary.

security-smoke-checks.caption: Run: `npx playwright test tests/security --trace=on`. Every assertion here can return FAIL on a real regression — that is what separates a gate from decoration.

security-smoke-checks.text: The senior tell is scope, not coverage. A smoke check that tries to be a full security scan becomes slow and flaky and gets muted within a sprint. Pick three or four invariants a reviewer would sign as 'must never regress on this flow', make them fast and deterministic, and block on them. Depth belongs in the scheduled scan; the gate exists to be trusted and to stay green until something genuinely broke.

security-smoke-checks.question: A reviewer challenges: 'How do I know this security smoke check is proven, not just described?' Which answer actually proves it?
options: The spec file exists and lists auth, header, and exposure tests with clear names.
The suite is green in CI on the current build, so the flow is secure.
You inject a regression (remove the ownership check) on a branch, show the authz test goes RED and blocks the release, then restore it and show it goes GREEN — captured in the trace.
The team agreed in review that the invariants are the right ones.
security-smoke-checks.explanation: Proof of a gate is demonstrated FAIL-then-PASS: a green suite (2) only shows the current build is clean, not that the check can catch anything, and existence (1) or agreement (4) prove intent, not capability. Injecting the regression and watching the gate turn red — then green after repair — is the executable evidence that the check separates safe from unsafe. A check never observed failing might be asserting nothing.

security-smoke-checks.intro: Prove your security smoke gate is real, not decoration:
items: For every invariant, name the exact regression that turns it RED (e.g. 'ownership check removed → 200 with line_items'). If you cannot, the assertion isn't guarding anything.
Inject one regression on a branch and confirm the matching test actually fails and blocks CI — a check never seen failing may be asserting nothing.
Confirm each check is deterministic: fixed target, seeded/known fixtures, no reliance on wall-clock or random data, so a red result means a real defect and not a flake.
Confirm the gate is fast enough to run on every release candidate (seconds, not the full scan) — a slow gate gets skipped under deadline pressure.
Capture trace/response evidence on failure so a reviewer can replay the exact leaked payload or missing header, and file the result as a defect report tied to the CI gate decision.

security-smoke-checks.title: Two 'security smoke checks' for the same checkout flow
security-smoke-checks.subtitle: Both look like security tests in review. Only one can catch a regression.

left.label: Describes security (weak)
lines: 'Log in, add to cart, check out' — happy path only
Drives the app as an authorized user throughout
No request the app is supposed to REJECT
No header or response-body assertion
Never observed failing; green tells you nothing
left.verdict: Passes locally, ships an IDOR to prod

right.label: Proves security (gold)
lines: Anon hits authed order route → expects 401/403 AND empty body
Asserts HSTS, nosniff, CSP present on the page
Asserts no PAN / no secret fields in the order response
Deterministic target + seeded fixtures — no flake
Regression injected once → went RED and blocked release
right.verdict: Blocks the release the weak suite waved through

security-smoke-checks.caption: The signal is the FAIL path: a check that only exercises what should work is a functional test wearing a security label. The gold version sends what should be refused and asserts the refusal.

prompts: In your own words: why does a fully green functional E2E suite tell you almost nothing about whether a flow is still secure?
Explain, using one assertion from your own gate, why a check that can only PASS is theater — and what the FAIL path proves.
Which of your invariants (authz, header, exposure) would a stricter environment force you to add or tighten, and what regression does that new check catch?

security-smoke-checks.text: The move is domain-independent: name a few invariants that must never regress, and write checks that can catch it when they do. A regulated fintech release tightens the gate — it adds an audit-log-written assertion, a stricter no-PII-in-logs probe, and a break-glass authz test, because the cost of a silent exposure is a fine, not a bug. A small team runs the same three probes but on merge instead of on a dedicated pipeline. What stays invariant everywhere: the check must be fast, deterministic, and able to turn red — and you must have watched it turn red at least once. Carry sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md into the capstone as the reusable proof that your release gate catches security regressions, not just functional ones.

ci-quality-gates.outcome: Take a revenue-critical web flow whose release is blocked by flaky browser tests and untriaged accessibility defects, and write the CI Quality Gate decision packet: the operating constraint, the gate you would enforce, the rejected option, the failure it would catch, and a flake-repair rule — grounded in real Playwright evidence, not vibes.
ci-quality-gates.proof: sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md: a constraint table, selected gate policy, rejected option, expected failure (tests green locally / red in CI), a verification hook (Playwright trace or CI gate result), a flake-triage rule, and one reviewer objection with its answer. A reviewer can replay the failure and evaluate the repair.
ci-quality-gates.unlock: Your packet names the constraint before the gate, attaches at least one inspection-hook output, and states what would make the gate DECISION invalid.
ci-quality-gates.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have a 'quality gate' if your gate only re-runs flaky tests until they pass. Auto-retry that hides flake is a gate that certifies noise. A real gate separates a true regression from a flaky selector — and can block on either.

ci-quality-gates.text: It is release day for checkout. The build is red — but two of the three failures are a login test that flakes on a slow selector, and the third is a real color-contrast defect on the Pay button. The room wants to click 'merge anyway.' The gate is the only thing standing between 'ship confidently' and 'ship blind.'

A CI quality gate turns 'the tests are red' into a release DECISION: block, quarantine, or ship-with-risk — backed by evidence a reviewer can inspect. It is the lesson where the flaky-test pain and the accessibility pain from earlier in this module finally get a policy that either lets a release through or stops it.

ci-quality-gates.prompt: Your checkout suite is red in CI but green on your laptop. Fastest safe move: re-run the job until it goes green, or something else? Decide before reading.
ci-quality-gates.reveal: Re-running to green is how flake ships to production. Local-green / CI-red almost always means a weak assumption — a race on a selector, a timing gap, a missing fixture, an env difference — not a broken machine. The expert move is to pull the Playwright trace for the ONE failing step and read what actually happened, so you can tell a real regression from a flaky locator. 'Green after retries' is not proof; it is a coin flip you called.

ci-quality-gates.title: A gate is a release decision backed by classified evidence — not a green checkmark
ci-quality-gates.text: A CI quality gate reads each failure, classifies it (true regression · flaky test · real a11y defect), and either blocks, quarantines the flake, or ships with a named risk. The invariant: a gate can say 'no,' and every 'yes' cites evidence a reviewer can replay.

ci-quality-gates.title: The CI quality gate — from red build to release decision
ci-quality-gates.subtitle: A failing checkout run enters the gate; each failure is classified from its Playwright trace, then routed. Regressions and unfixed a11y defects BLOCK; a confirmed flake is quarantined; a clean run ships. The gate always emits an inspectable evidence bundle.

legend.label: ship with an inspectable evidence bundle

ci-quality-gates.title: The gate as a Playwright CI config + policy
ci-quality-gates.subtitle: The real artifact from the packet: a config that PRODUCES evidence and a gate that classifies it — no retry-to-green.

steps.label: One retry to DETECT, not to hide
steps.note: A single CI retry lets you observe flake. But a test that only passes on the retry is not a pass — line 30 treats it as FLAKE. This is the whole discipline: retry to classify, never to launder.

steps.label: Emit replayable evidence
steps.note: trace + screenshot + video on failure are the proof the gate and a reviewer replay. `npx playwright show-report` opens the trace for the exact failing step.

steps.label: Machine-readable result
steps.note: The JSON report is what the gate parses. A gate that reads console output instead of structured results is guessing.

steps.label: Accessibility is a gated project
steps.note: The a11y scan is not a nice-to-have side job — it is its own project the gate can BLOCK on, so an untriaged contrast defect cannot slip through with a green functional suite.

steps.label: The load-bearing rule
steps.note: `passed && retry > 0 → FLAKE`. This single line is what separates a real gate from a retry loop. Green-after-retry becomes a quarantine ticket, not a ship signal.

steps.label: Classify, then route
steps.note: A11y failures and regressions both block; only confirmed flake is quarantined. The gate returns a class, and the CI step maps class → block / quarantine / ship.

ci-quality-gates.caption: Run: newest CI job shows login.spec passed only on retry (FLAKE → quarantine) and pay-button.a11y.spec failed on contrast (A11Y_DEFECT → BLOCK). The gate says no — with a trace you can open.

ci-quality-gates.text: The senior tell is what the gate does with a test that passed on retry. A weak gate calls it green and ships. A real gate calls it FLAKE, files a quarantine ticket, and keeps the flake OUT of the release-blocking suite while it is fixed — so the gate stays trustworthy. A gate everyone routinely overrides is not a gate; it is a suggestion with a red icon.

ci-quality-gates.question: A reviewer challenges: 'How do I know your CI quality gate is proven, not just described?' Which packet earns the merge?
options: The gate is green because the pipeline retried the checkout suite three times until it passed.

The gate blocked on a Playwright trace showing a real regression AND an a11y contrast failure, quarantined one confirmed flake with a ticket, and shipped only after both blockers were resolved — every decision citing replayable evidence.
The packet explains gate policy in the abstract and lists best practices, but shows no failing run and no trace.
The gate passed the suite locally, so CI redness was waved through as an environment quirk.
ci-quality-gates.explanation: A gate is proven only when a reviewer can replay the failure and evaluate the repair. Option 2 classifies each failure from trace evidence, blocks on the real regression and the a11y defect, quarantines the flake instead of retrying it to green, and ships with an inspectable bundle. Retrying to green (1) and 'environment quirk' (4) launder flake into a false pass; abstract best practices (3) is the weak version — described, never proven.

ci-quality-gates.title: Retry-to-green vs a real quality gate
ci-quality-gates.subtitle: Same red checkout build. Both end 'green.' Only one is safe to ship.

left.label: Retry until it passes
lines: retries: 5 — rerun the suite until CI goes green
No trace read; nobody knows WHY it was red
Flaky login test counted as a genuine pass
Accessibility scan not gated — contrast defect ships
'Green after retries' presented as proof
Local-green used to wave off CI-red
left.verdict: Certifies noise — ships flake + the a11y defect

right.label: Classify, block, quarantine
lines: retries: 1 to DETECT flake, never to hide it
trace: retain-on-failure — every failure is replayable
passed-on-retry → FLAKE → quarantine ticket, not PASS
a11y is a gated project — contrast defect BLOCKS
Regression blocks; ship only after both resolved
Evidence bundle a reviewer can open and challenge
right.verdict: Blocks real breaks — ships with proof, not hope

ci-quality-gates.caption: The invalidation condition: any run where the gate looks green in review but was green only because retries buried a flake or the a11y project was never gated.

ci-quality-gates.intro: Prove your gate holds — no vibes:
items: Open the Playwright trace for each failing step (npx playwright show-report). If you cannot point to the exact action that failed, you are guessing, not gating.
Confirm a test that passed only on retry is classified FLAKE and routed to quarantine — not counted as a pass. If retries can turn red into ship, your gate launders noise.
Confirm the accessibility scan is a gated project that can BLOCK, and that the untriaged contrast defect is either fixed or explicitly ship-blocking — never silently green.
State the operating constraint the gate serves (e.g. 'no daytime downtime on the revenue path') and name one option it rules out — a gate with no constraint is decoration.
Write the invalidation condition: the exact result that would prove this gate certified a release it should have blocked. If you can't, the gate isn't falsifiable.

prompts: Explain, using your own packet, why 'green after retries' is not proof a release is safe — and what your gate does with a passed-on-retry test instead.
Walk a junior through classifying one real failure from its Playwright trace: how did you tell a true regression from a flaky selector?
Why is the accessibility check a first-class gated project and not a side job? Name the constraint it protects and the defect class it would block.

ci-quality-gates.text: The same gate logic — read the evidence, classify the failure, block or quarantine, ship only with proof — reshapes with the environment. On a two-person team the gate might be a single required check with a manual flake ticket; in a regulated enterprise it adds a signed audit trail and a sign-off before override; at high scale it needs a flake-detection service and per-shard quarantine so one bad selector can't block a thousand PRs. What stays invariant: a passed-on-retry test is never a pass, and every 'ship' cites a trace a reviewer can open. Carry sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md into the capstone — it is your portfolio proof that you can turn a red build into a defensible release decision, not just 'I understand CI gates.'

flaky-test-triage.outcome: Take one real flaky Playwright test that blocks a revenue-critical web flow and produce a triage decision: name the flake class, quarantine-or-fix call, the trace evidence that proves it, and the CI quality-gate rule that keeps it from re-blocking the release.
flaky-test-triage.proof: sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md: a constraint line, the flake class (timing / selector / fixture / environment), the selected approach, the rejected approach, the Playwright trace/screenshot/video that proves the cause, the CI gate decision, and one reviewer objection you answered. A second reviewer can replay the trace and reach your verdict.
flaky-test-triage.unlock: Your packet names the flake class, attaches trace evidence, and states a CI-gate rule — with a rejected option written down, not implied.
flaky-test-triage.doNotClaim: Do not claim a test is 'fixed' because a re-run went green. Green-on-retry is the definition of flaky, not proof of repair. Without a trace that shows the root cause and a gate that catches the class, you quarantined luck, not the defect.

flaky-test-triage.text: The release train is held: the checkout browser test failed CI, passed on retry, failed again on the next PR. Three engineers are arguing 'just add a retry' while the accessibility defects behind it stay untriaged — and nobody can say whether the flake is timing, a selector, or the environment.

A flaky test is a test that passes and fails on the same code — so it stops being a release signal and becomes noise the whole team learns to ignore. Flaky test triage is the ownership move that converts 'it failed again' into a named class, a proof, and a gate the next PR inherits.

flaky-test-triage.prompt: A checkout test passes locally every time but fails ~1 in 4 CI runs. Your teammate says 'flake — add retries: 2 and move on.' Before you agree — what does that actually buy you?
flaky-test-triage.reveal: It buys silence, not signal. Retries mask the class instead of naming it: if the cause is a race between click and a not-yet-hydrated button, retry hides a real user-facing bug that also fails 1-in-4 for customers. The expert move is to separate signal from noise first — read the trace, classify the flake (timing / selector / fixture / environment), and only THEN decide quarantine vs fix. Retry-first is a decision that looks like triage.

flaky-test-triage.code:
# Flake Triage & Quality-Gate Packet
## Constraint: no daytime downtime; release blocked; fix must land this PR cycle
## Symptom: checkout 'Place order' test — green locally, RED ~1/4 in CI
## Flake class: TIMING (race: click fires before button is hydrated/enabled)
## Evidence: trace shows click at 812ms, button [disabled] until 1140ms
##   npx playwright test --trace=on && npx playwright show-report
## Rejected: retries:2 in config — masks a real 1/4 user-facing failure
## Selected: replace fixed wait + raw click with a web-first assertion
#   - await expect(page.getByRole('button',{name:'Place order'})).toBeEnabled()
#   - await page.getByRole('button',{name:'Place order'}).click()
## Proof: re-ran --repeat-each=20 --project=chromium -> 20/20 green
## CI gate: fail the pipeline if @flaky-tagged count > 3 OR flake-rate > 1%
## Reviewer objection: 'proven or just re-run lucky?' -> trace + 20x answer it
## Transfer: same class in a regulated env -> quarantine first, fix under change ticket

steps.label: State the constraint first
steps.note: Ownership starts here: the release is blocked and there is no daytime-downtime window. The constraint rules out slow fixes before you pick one.

steps.label: Name the flake class
steps.note: Timing / selector / fixture / environment. 'Timing' is a classification you can act on; 'it's flaky' is not.

steps.label: Prove the cause from the trace
steps.note: The trace timestamps are the signal: the click fired at 812ms while the button stayed [disabled] until 1140ms — a race, directly observed, not inferred.

steps.label: Write the rejected option
steps.note: retries:2 would have gone green and hidden a failure real customers hit 1-in-4. Recording why you rejected it is what makes this triage, not a guess.

steps.label: The repair: a web-first assertion
steps.note: Playwright's expect().toBeEnabled() auto-waits and retries the assertion — it removes the race instead of papering over it with a sleep.

steps.label: Prove the repair
steps.note: --repeat-each=20 green is the flake-specific proof. One green run is the flake's natural state; 20/20 is evidence.

steps.label: The CI quality gate
steps.note: The class-level defense: the pipeline fails if the @flaky budget or flake-rate is exceeded, so this class cannot silently re-block a future release.

flaky-test-triage.caption: A reviewer replays --trace=on, sees the 812ms-vs-1140ms race, and reaches your verdict without you narrating.

flaky-test-triage.caption: Green-on-retry is the flake's definition, not its cure. The trace + 20x re-run is the only proof that survives a reviewer challenge.

flaky-test-triage.text: The senior tell: never delete or blanket-retry a flake before you can name its class from the trace. A quarantine WITH an owned fix ticket and a flake-budget gate is disciplined; a silent retries:2 is technical debt that costs you the release signal. If your test can only pass, it is theater — a real check must be able to fail for a real reason.

flaky-test-triage.question: A reviewer challenges your triage: 'How do I know this flake is actually fixed and not just re-run lucky?' Which evidence answers them?
options: The test passed on the last CI run, so it is fixed.
You added retries: 2, so intermittent failures no longer block the pipeline.
The trace shows the named cause (click-before-enabled), the fix is a web-first assertion, and --repeat-each=20 returned 20/20 green.
You increased the global timeout from 30s to 60s so the test has more time.
flaky-test-triage.explanation: Only option 3 is inspectable proof of a class: a trace that names the cause, a fix that targets it, and a repeated-run result that a flake's natural randomness cannot fake. One green run (1) is the flake's baseline; retries (2) and a longer timeout (4) both hide the class rather than proving it repaired.

flaky-test-triage.intro: Prove your triage packet holds — no green-on-retry vibes:
items: Your packet names ONE flake class (timing, selector, fixture, or environment) — 'it's flaky' is not a class; re-read the trace until you can name it.
The cause is shown in trace/screenshot/video evidence a reviewer can replay, not asserted in prose.
The rejected option is written down (e.g. blanket retries) with why it fails under the no-downtime constraint.
The repair is proven flake-specifically: --repeat-each or a 20x re-run returns all-green, not a single pass.
A CI quality-gate rule (flake-rate threshold or @flaky budget) is stated, so the class cannot silently re-block the next release.

prompts: In your own words: why is 'the test passed on retry' the definition of a flake rather than evidence it is fixed?
Explain the difference between quarantining a flake and blanket-retrying it — using your own packet, name when quarantine is the disciplined call.
Point to the exact trace evidence in your packet and say what flake class it proves and what would INVALIDATE that classification.

flaky-test-triage.text: The same triage travels wherever a signal goes noisy. A smaller team may quarantine and ship faster because the blast radius is small; a regulated enterprise environment forbids quarantining a revenue path silently — you fix under a change ticket with the trace attached as the audit record; a high-scale product hits environment-class flakes (shared test data, parallel-run contention) that never appear locally, so the fixture strategy becomes the fix. What stays invariant: classify from evidence, prove the repair with repeated runs, and gate the class. Carry sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md into the capstone — the review board reuses this exact artifact and its trace as your proof that the release signal is trustworthy.

bug-reports.outcome: Take one real (or realistic) failing test on a revenue-critical web flow and write a bug report that a reviewer can ACT on without a follow-up question: exact reproduction, expected vs actual, environment (local vs CI), attached Playwright trace/screenshot/video, severity, and a flake-vs-real-defect verdict.
bug-reports.proof: sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md: a single defect entry with steps to reproduce, expected/actual, environment, attached trace evidence (npx playwright test --trace=on), severity, and an explicit "flake or real defect" call with the evidence that decides it. A reviewer reproduces it on the first read.
bug-reports.unlock: Your bug report reproduces on first read, distinguishes flake from real defect with trace evidence, and states a severity a release manager can gate on.
bug-reports.doNotClaim: Do not claim a bug is "reported" if the entry is just "login is broken, see screenshot." That is a complaint, not a report. A report carries the exact steps, the environment where it fails, the trace, and whether the failure is deterministic — enough for someone else to reproduce and decide without asking you a single question.

bug-reports.text: Release day, the checkout suite goes red in CI but green on every laptop in the room. Three engineers argue "it's just flaky" versus "it's a real defect" for an hour — because nobody attached a trace, and the bug report says only "cart test failed sometimes."

A bug report is the interface between finding a failure and someone fixing it — the artifact that turns a red pipeline into a decision. When it is shallow, tests pass locally but fail in CI, and the whole team relitigates the same failure instead of repairing it once.

bug-reports.prompt: A Playwright test failed in CI but passes locally. Before you file anything — is the FIRST job to describe the bug, or to decide something else? Answer before reading on.
bug-reports.reveal: First job: decide flake or real defect — because that verdict changes everything downstream. A real defect blocks the release and needs a code fix; a flake needs a stabilized locator/wait, not a rollback. The evidence that decides it (trace, retry count, timing) IS the core of the report. File "login broken" without that verdict and you have handed the reader your homework: they must now re-run, re-triage, and re-decide what you already had the trace to prove.

bug-reports.title: A bug report is reproducible evidence plus a flake-vs-defect verdict
bug-reports.text: Exact steps, expected vs actual, the environment it fails in, and an attached trace — then the call that decides action: deterministic real defect (fix + gate) or environment/timing flake (stabilize + quarantine). Evidence carries the verdict; the reader never re-triages.

bug-reports.code:
# Bug Report — checkout: add-to-cart intermittently loses item

- ID / Suite: BUG-1471 · e2e/checkout.spec.ts > 'adds item to cart'
- Environment: FAILS in CI (chromium, GitHub Actions) · PASSES local (headed)
- Steps to reproduce:
  1. seed cart-empty fixture, goto /product/SKU-88
  2. click [data-testid="add-to-cart"]
  3. assert cart badge == "1"
- Expected: cart badge shows "1" within 2s
- Actual: badge stays "0"; assertion times out at 5s (CI only)
- Evidence: trace.zip (npx playwright test --trace=on) · screenshot · video
- Trace autopsy: click fired BEFORE the add-to-cart XHR handler bound (race)
- Verdict: REAL DEFECT (deterministic in CI's slower cold-start), not flake
- Severity: S1 — blocks primary revenue flow → CI gate: RED, hold release
- Repair: await response('/api/cart') as web-first assertion, not fixed sleep

steps.label: ID + exact test path
steps.note: Name the suite and test so the reader opens the same failure you saw — not "the checkout tests".

steps.label: Environment: where it fails
steps.note: "Fails in CI, passes local" is the single most important line — it points straight at timing, fixture, or environment assumptions, the class this course exists to fix.

steps.label: Steps + fixture state
steps.note: Start from a named fixture (cart-empty), not a live shared DB. Reproduction that depends on hidden state is not reproduction.

steps.label: Expected vs actual
steps.note: Both concrete and observable. "Badge stays 0, times out at 5s" is a dashboard-recognizable fact; "cart broken" is a vibe.

steps.label: Attach the trace
steps.note: trace.zip from --trace=on is the reviewer's replay button. A report without it makes them re-run to see what you already saw.

steps.label: Trace autopsy → the verdict
steps.note: The trace shows the click raced the XHR binding: deterministic under CI's slower cold-start. That evidence turns "sometimes fails" into REAL DEFECT, not flake — the call that routes the fix.

steps.label: Severity + gate + repair
steps.note: S1 blocks the revenue flow, so the CI gate goes red. The repair is a web-first assertion (await the response), never a fixed sleep — sleeps are how flakes are born.

bug-reports.caption: A reviewer reads this once, replays trace.zip, and reproduces the S1 without asking you anything.
