bug-reports.caption: The verdict (flake vs real defect) plus the trace is what turns a report from "more work for the reader" into "a decision the reader can sign."

bug-reports.text: The senior tell in a bug report is the flake-vs-defect verdict backed by a trace — not the prose. Anyone can write "login is broken." A release manager trusts the engineer who writes "deterministic in CI's cold-start, here's the trace of the race, S1, gate it" — because that report already did the triage the reader would otherwise have to redo at 2 a.m. on release day.

bug-reports.question: A Playwright checkout test fails in CI but passes locally. Which bug report is actually actionable?
options: "Checkout is flaky in CI, please look into it when you get a chance."

"add-to-cart fails only in CI (chromium): steps + cart-empty fixture attached, expected badge=1 vs actual badge=0 timing out at 5s, trace.zip shows the click races the XHR binding — REAL DEFECT, S1, gate red."
"The test suite is red again, probably the usual flakiness, just rerun it."
"Something's wrong with the cart, I attached a screenshot of the failure."
bug-reports.explanation: Only option 2 pins the environment (CI-only), reproduces from a named fixture, states expected vs actual concretely, attaches a trace, and — critically — delivers the flake-vs-defect verdict with the evidence that decides it and a severity a gate can act on. The others are complaints: they hand the reader the triage instead of the decision, which is exactly how 'passes locally, fails in CI' festers.

bug-reports.intro: Prove your bug report is actionable — no vibes:
items: Hand the report to a peer with no context. If they can reproduce the failure without asking you one question, the steps + fixture + environment are complete; if not, a field is missing.
Confirm the environment line names WHERE it fails (local vs CI, which browser/project) — the 'passes local, fails in CI' signal is the most diagnostic line in the report.
Check that a Playwright trace/screenshot/video is attached (npx playwright test --trace=on, npx playwright show-report) — evidence the reader can replay, not prose they must trust.
Confirm the flake-vs-real-defect verdict is stated AND backed by evidence (retry behavior, trace autopsy, timing) — not left as an open question for the reader.
Check the severity maps to a CI gate decision (block release vs quarantine + stabilize), so a release manager can act on it directly.

prompts: In your own words: why does the 'fails in CI, passes locally' line tell a fixer more than the assertion message itself?
Explain the difference between a flake and a real defect using your own report — and name the exact trace evidence that decided which one you filed.
Walk a junior through why an attached trace changes a bug report from 'trust me' to 'reproduce it yourself,' and why that changes how fast it gets fixed.

bug-reports.text: The same discipline scales up and down. On a two-person team the bug report can be a Slack thread — but it still needs steps, environment, evidence, and a flake-vs-defect verdict, or you relitigate it tomorrow. In a regulated enterprise, that same report becomes an audit artifact: the trace and the CI gate decision are the evidence a release was allowed to ship. At high scale, the report feeds automated flake triage and quarantine — the verdict field is what a bot reads to decide quarantine vs block. What stays invariant everywhere: a bug report is reproducible evidence carrying a decision, never a complaint. This exact sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md is the artifact your capstone reuses — the defect entry, the trace, and the gate call are the proof that your automation caught a real risk without shipping false confidence.

release-risk-scoring.outcome: Take a revenue-critical web flow whose release is blocked by flaky browser tests and untriaged accessibility defects, and score the release: rate each risk axis, pick ship | hold | conditional-ship, and record the one condition that would flip the call. Write it as a decision packet a reviewer can replay.
release-risk-scoring.proof: sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md: a scored risk table (severity × likelihood × detectability per axis), the selected gate decision, the rejected option, the flake autopsy, the a11y result, and the CI gate result. A reviewer can point to a score, replay the failing Playwright trace, and challenge whether the number is proven or guessed.
release-risk-scoring.unlock: Your packet scores each risk axis with evidence, names the gate decision + the rejected option, and states the exact signal that would invalidate the score.
release-risk-scoring.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'scored the release' if the score is a single gut number with no axis breakdown and no evidence behind it. A risk score a reviewer cannot trace to a trace, a contract check, or an a11y result is a vibe with a decimal point — not a release gate.

release-risk-scoring.text: It is release night on the checkout flow. Two Playwright specs are red — but they were red yesterday too, and green the run before that. The VP asks the one question that decides revenue: 'Is that a real bug, or is the test lying?' The room that can score the difference ships; the room that can't either blocks good code or leaks a real defect to production.

A red test is not the same as a shipping decision — a flaky spec and a genuine regression both show up red. Release risk scoring converts a wall of raw pass/fail signal into one defensible gate call, backed by the trace, contract, and a11y evidence a reviewer can replay.

release-risk-scoring.prompt: Two specs fail in CI but pass on your laptop. Same commit. Before you touch anything — is that a safer release or a riskier one than two specs failing everywhere? Decide before reading on.
release-risk-scoring.reveal: Riskier — because 'passes locally, fails in CI' is the exact signature of weak assumptions: race-prone locators, timing waits, unseeded fixtures, environment drift. A failure that reproduces everywhere is at least honest; you can diagnose it. A failure that only appears in CI hides which side is lying — the test or the code — so your risk score has to account for detectability, not just whether it's red. The dangerous release isn't the one with red tests; it's the one where you can't tell flaky from broken.

release-risk-scoring.title: A release risk score rates each axis on evidence, then gates the ship
release-risk-scoring.text: For every risk axis — flaky specs, contract drift, a11y defects — score severity × likelihood × detectability from replayable evidence, not gut. The gate decision follows the scores; the invariant: every number traces to a trace, a contract check, or an a11y result.

release-risk-scoring.title: The release risk scoring pipeline
release-risk-scoring.subtitle: Raw CI signal → per-axis scoring against evidence → one gate decision. The flaky-spec axis feeds a triage branch: quarantine (real flake) vs block (real regression). Payments latency and copy are deliberately out of scope for this gate.

release-risk-scoring.code:
# SDET Quality Gate & Flake Repair Packet — checkout release
Context: revenue-critical checkout flow; release blocked by 2 red specs + 3 a11y defects.

## Risk scores (severity 1-5 × likelihood 1-5 × detectability 1-5 = score)
| Axis            | Sev | Lik | Det | Score | Evidence hook                                  |
|-----------------|-----|-----|-----|-------|------------------------------------------------|
| Flaky specs     |  2  |  4  |  2  |  16   | npx playwright test --trace=on -> show-report  |
| Contract drift  |  5  |  2  |  4  |  40   | POST /api/checkout schema snapshot diff        |
| A11y defects    |  4  |  5  |  3  |  60   | axe scan: cart total has no accessible name    |

## Triage (flaky axis): trace stable across retries, only a 500ms timing wait failed
-> classify as FLAKE, quarantine spec `checkout.spec.ts:payButton`, file repair ticket

## Selected gate: CONDITIONAL-SHIP
- Rejected: hard BLOCK on all red (would block on a proven flake -> false confidence cost)
- Condition to flip to HOLD: any a11y defect on the pay button itself (blocks screen readers from paying)

## Invalidation: score is void if the flaky trace later reproduces a real state change
## CI gate result: quarantined flake = amber, a11y P1 = red until fixed -> gate HOLDS on a11y

steps.label: Score three axes, not one
steps.note: Severity × likelihood × detectability — the third factor is what beginners drop. A low-detectability risk (you can't easily see it) is scarier at the same severity.

steps.label: The flaky-spec row
steps.note: High likelihood, LOW detectability (2) — you often can't tell flaky from broken. That low score of 16 is honest only because the trace resolved it.

steps.label: The contract-drift row
steps.note: Severity 5: a checkout schema break loses money silently. High score even at low likelihood — severity dominates when the failure is invisible to users until it's too late.

steps.label: Every score cites a hook
steps.note: No number without `--trace=on`, a schema diff, or an axe scan behind it. This column is what makes the score replayable instead of asserted.

steps.label: Triage the flake, don't just block
steps.note: Replay the trace across retries. Stable trace + a lone timing wait = flake → quarantine it. A test that can only ever say 'red' teaches the gate nothing.

steps.label: The gate + the rejected option + the flip condition
steps.note: Conditional-ship, NOT block-on-all-red (that penalizes proven flakes). Name what would move it to HOLD — here, an a11y defect on the pay button itself.

release-risk-scoring.caption: A reviewer replays the flaky trace, confirms the flake classification, checks the a11y score against the axe output, and sees exactly why the gate still HOLDS — on accessibility, not on the flake.

left.label: Gut-feel call
lines: "Feels risky" / "should be fine" — no scale
One loud bug dominates; quiet risks ignored
No weighting by impact or blast radius
Decision changes with whoever is in the room
No record of why you shipped
left.verdict: Un-auditable; ships the wrong risk

right.label: Scored release risk
lines: Each risk = likelihood x impact on a fixed scale
Weighted by blast radius (revenue path first)
Open-defect severity + coverage gaps folded in
A threshold gating ship vs hold vs rollback-ready
The score + its inputs recorded for the postmortem
right.verdict: Defensible number a reviewer can replay

release-risk-scoring.caption: A release-risk score is the decision made inspectable — the same signals, weighted and written down.

release-risk-scoring.text: The senior tell in a review board: a mid SDET reports 'tests are red, we can't ship.' A senior reports 'the two red specs are a quarantined flake — trace attached — but a P1 a11y defect on the pay button blocks the gate.' Same red dashboard; one score separates signal from noise and names the ONE risk actually holding the release.

release-risk-scoring.question: Your risk packet says the flaky-spec axis scores low. The review board pushes back: 'Prove that's a flake and not a real regression you're waving through.' What is the exact evidence that answers them?
options: The spec passed on your laptop three times in a row, so it's clearly the CI environment.
A Playwright trace replayed across retries shows a stable DOM/state — only a timing wait failed — so the code path is unchanged; you quarantine the spec and file a repair ticket.
You re-ran the whole suite and it went green this time.
The spec has failed intermittently for weeks, so everyone already agrees it's flaky.
release-risk-scoring.explanation: Only option 2 is replayable evidence a reviewer can inspect: the trace shows the application state was identical across retries and only a timing assertion flaked — that distinguishes a flake from a masked regression. 'Passed on my laptop' (1) is the exact failure signature you're supposed to distrust; a lucky green re-run (3) proves nothing; and 'everyone agrees' (4) is social proof, not a trace.

release-risk-scoring.intro: Prove your release risk score is real — no vibes:
items: Every axis has three factors scored (severity, likelihood, detectability), not one lump number — and detectability is not silently maxed out.
Every score cites a replayable hook: a --trace=on report, a contract/schema diff, or an axe/a11y scan. A score with no evidence column is deleted, not defended.
The flaky axis was triaged by replaying the trace, and each red spec is classified flake-quarantine or real-block — not left ambiguous.
The gate decision (ship | hold | conditional-ship) names the rejected option AND the one condition that would flip it.
You wrote the invalidation line: the exact future signal that would prove this score wrong (e.g. the 'flaky' trace later shows a real state change).

prompts: In your own words: why is detectability a separate risk factor from severity and likelihood — and give an example from your packet where a low-detectability risk outranked a more likely one.
Explain how you told a flake apart from a real regression using the Playwright trace, using your own quarantined spec as the example.
Your gate said conditional-ship. Name the one condition that would flip it to hold, and why that specific signal — not the red tests generally — is the real risk.

release-risk-scoring.text: This is portfolio evidence, not a worksheet: 'here is a release I scored — flaky specs quarantined with traces, an a11y defect that actually held the gate, and the condition that would have flipped it.' The same scoring moves to a stricter environment and change what you'd expect: in a regulated enterprise release, detectability weights heaviest (an undetected defect is an audit finding) and 'conditional-ship' often isn't allowed; on a high-scale product, likelihood dominates because a 0.1% flow failure is thousands of users. What stays invariant is the spine — score each axis on replayable evidence, triage flake from regression by trace, and let the gate follow the numbers. Carry this packet into the capstone; the review board reuses it verbatim.

quality-review-board.outcome: Convene a Quality Review Board for a real (or realistic) release blocked by flaky browser tests and untriaged accessibility defects. Produce a signed release-gate decision packet: the constraint, the ship/hold call, the rejected option, the flake and a11y evidence, and the reversal condition — all inspectable by another reviewer.
quality-review-board.proof: sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md plus quality_review_board_risk_register.md: a constraint table, the gate verdict, a Playwright trace/report reference, an accessibility result, a CI gate decision, one rejected option, and the top three residual risks. A second reviewer can replay the flake and re-derive the same verdict without you narrating.
quality-review-board.unlock: Your board turns the raw release risk into a gate verdict backed by executable evidence (trace, a11y check, CI result), names the rejected option, and states what would reverse the decision.
quality-review-board.doNotClaim: Do not claim a Quality Review Board 'approved the release' if the packet only describes quality in the abstract. A gate with no replayable flake evidence and no accessibility result is a rubber stamp, not a review. The board owns the decision and the proof, not a vibe that 'tests looked green'.

quality-review-board.text: Friday, 4 p.m., a revenue-critical checkout flow is one merge from release — but three browser tests failed twice and passed once, and two accessibility defects sit untriaged. The room wants a thumbs-up; the Quality Review Board asks the only question that matters: 'Is this flakiness or a real regression, and can a keyboard user still check out?'

A Quality Review Board is where an SDET converts product risk into an inspectable release decision — separating flake from regression, triaging conformance defects, and gating on evidence a reviewer can replay. It sits at the end of SDET Operations: the last checkpoint before revenue-critical code ships.

quality-review-board.prompt: A checkout test failed in CI but passes when you re-run it locally. The board is asked to sign off because 'it's just flaky.' What is wrong with shipping on that reasoning? Answer before reading on.
quality-review-board.reveal: 'Just flaky' is an untriaged verdict wearing a decision's clothes. Local pass proves nothing — CI differs in timing, viewport, network, and fixture state, which is exactly where checkout regressions hide. The board's job is to open the Playwright trace, watch the failed step, and prove it was a timing/selector flake and NOT a real broken 'Place order' button. Calling it flake without the trace is how a revenue regression ships behind a green-looking dashboard.

quality-review-board.title: A review board gates on replayable evidence, not on a green dashboard
quality-review-board.text: The Quality Review Board converts release risk into one verdict — ship, hold, or fix — backed by evidence any reviewer can replay: a Playwright trace that separates flake from regression, an accessibility result, and a CI gate decision. The invariant: no evidence, no gate.

quality-review-board.title: The Quality Review Board as a release-gate decision flow
quality-review-board.subtitle: Release candidate → three evidence streams (flake triage · accessibility · contract) → board verdict. The suspect edge is flaky browser tests feeding a false-green CI gate; the blast radius is a broken checkout shipping to revenue.

legend.label: the gate verdict — ship / hold / fix

quality-review-board.title: The flake-triage evidence that unblocks the gate
quality-review-board.subtitle: Reproduce the failure under trace, then read the trace to prove flake vs regression — the exact move the board demands before a verdict.
quality-review-board.code:
# 1. Reproduce the exact CI failure locally, WITH a trace on every run
npx playwright test checkout.spec.ts \
  --project=chromium \
  --retries=0 \
  --repeat-each=5 \
  --trace=on

# 2. Open the trace for the failed attempt — watch the step that broke
npx playwright show-report

# Trace reading (what the board records in the packet):
#   step: getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }).click()
#   -> attempt 3/5 FAILED: element detached during re-render, click lost
#   -> attempts 1,2,4,5 PASSED: same selector, same assertion
#   VERDICT: FLAKE (race on re-render), NOT a broken checkout button

# 3. Repair the flake at the root: web-first assertion waits for actionability
#   BEFORE: await page.locator('.btn-primary').click()          // brittle
#   AFTER:  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' })
#             .click()                                            // auto-waits

# 4. Prove the repair holds AND accessibility still passes the gate
npx playwright test checkout.spec.ts --repeat-each=10 --trace=on   # 10/10 green
npx playwright test a11y.spec.ts --grep @axe                       # keyboard + contrast

steps.label: Reproduce under trace, not vibes
steps.note: --repeat-each=5 --retries=0 forces the intermittent failure to surface; --trace=on captures the DOM, network, and each action so the board can watch what actually broke.

steps.label: Open the report and trace
steps.note: The trace viewer is the board's evidence exhibit. You do not argue 'it's flaky' — you point at the failed step and its screenshot timeline.

steps.label: Read the trace: flake or regression
steps.note: Same selector, same assertion, mixed pass/fail on a re-render race = flake. If ALL attempts failed on a missing button, that is a real checkout regression — HOLD the release.

steps.label: Repair at the root, not with a sleep
steps.note: A role-based locator with a web-first assertion auto-waits for actionability. Adding a fixed timeout would hide the flake, not kill it — the board rejects that repair.

steps.label: Prove the repair and re-check a11y
steps.note: 10/10 green under repeat proves the flake is dead; the axe run proves the keyboard/contrast defects the board flagged are actually cleared before ship.

quality-review-board.caption: The board's rule: a 'flake' claim is only accepted with a trace showing mixed pass/fail on an identical selector. Everything else is a regression until proven otherwise.

quality-review-board.title: Two review boards, same blocked release
quality-review-board.subtitle: Checkout is one merge from shipping, tests are flaky, two a11y defects untriaged. Both boards meet; only one produces an inspectable gate.

left.label: Rubber-stamp board
lines: 'Tests are flaky, re-run passed, ship it'
No trace opened — flake vs regression never separated
Accessibility defects deferred, untriaged, no severity
Verdict rests on a green-looking dashboard
No rejected option, no reversal condition recorded
left.verdict: Ships a possible checkout regression on faith

right.label: Evidence-gated board
lines: Trace proves mixed pass/fail on one selector = flake, repaired
axe result: keyboard defect = blocker, contrast = ship-with-ticket
CI gate decision recorded with the failing-then-green run IDs
Rejected option: 'ship and hotfix Monday' — violates revenue-flow constraint
Reversal condition: hold if repeat-each run drops below 10/10
right.verdict: Gate any reviewer can replay and re-derive

quality-review-board.caption: The gap is not effort — both boards met. The difference is that one gate is inspectable: a reviewer can replay the flake, read the a11y severity, and reach the same verdict.

quality-review-board.text: The senior tell in a review board is triage discipline: not every accessibility defect blocks a release, and not every red test is a regression. A blocker (keyboard user cannot complete checkout) holds the ship; a lower-severity defect (a decorative-image alt-text gap) ships with a filed ticket. A board that treats all defects as equal blocks forever; a board that treats them all as ignorable ships broken. The skill is the severity call — and defending it with evidence.

quality-review-board.question: The board is shown a checkout test that failed once in CI and passed on re-run. What is the minimum evidence required before recording a 'flake, safe to ship' verdict?
options: The engineer's statement that it passes locally now.

A Playwright trace of the failed run showing mixed pass/fail on the identical selector/assertion (a race), plus a repeat-each re-run that is green — proving the failure was non-deterministic, not a real regression.
A green CI dashboard on the latest run.
A comment in the PR saying 'known flaky, ignore.'
quality-review-board.explanation: Flake and regression look identical on a dashboard — the difference is only visible in the trace. A local pass (1), a single green run (3), or a hand-wave comment (4) cannot distinguish a timing race from a genuinely broken 'Place order' button. Only the trace showing an identical selector passing and failing non-deterministically, backed by a repeat-each green run, lets the board honestly certify flake rather than smuggle a revenue regression past the gate.

quality-review-board.intro: Prove your Quality Review Board gate holds — no rubber stamp:
items: Your packet contains a Playwright trace reference for every 'flake' verdict, showing mixed pass/fail on an identical selector — not just a re-run that happened to pass.
Every accessibility defect has a triaged severity (blocker vs ship-with-ticket) that you can defend, not a blanket 'defer'.
The CI gate decision is recorded with the concrete run IDs: the failing run and the green run that proves the repair.
One rejected option is written down with the constraint it violates (e.g. 'ship-and-hotfix' violates the no-broken-revenue-flow constraint).
A reversal condition is stated — the exact evidence that would flip ship back to hold (e.g. repeat-each drops below 10/10, or a11y blocker reopens).

prompts: In your own words: why can a board never certify 'flake' from a dashboard alone, and what does the trace add that the dashboard cannot?
Explain your severity call on one accessibility defect — why it was a blocker or ship-with-ticket — using your own packet as the example.
What is the one constraint your board refused to violate, and which tempting option (ship-and-hotfix, ignore-the-defect) did it eliminate?

quality-review-board.text: The review-board move — gate on replayable evidence, triage by severity, name the reversal condition — travels to any release checkpoint. On a small team the board is one SDET and a five-minute trace review; in a regulated enterprise it is a signed change-advisory record with an audit trail and a named approver; at high scale it is an automated merge queue where the flake-triage and axe checks ARE the gate and a human only reviews the holds. What changes is ceremony and who signs; what stays invariant is the rule that a verdict must rest on evidence a second person can replay. The packet you built — sdet_quality_gate_and_flake_repair_packet.md — is portfolio proof: not 'I understand quality gates' but 'here is a release I framed, triaged, gated, and could defend to any reviewer.' Carry it into the capstone, where this exact packet becomes the release decision for the full test-automation suite.
